speechtext: Hear, hear.

The Prime Minister thinks he is safe there, so he is willing to withdraw Quebec, but in Ontario, where lists have been prepared and the Prime Minister cannot say that anything has been wrongly done, he wants to have five or six members elected simply by this Bill. I am surprised that the Minister of Customs, who represents Ontario in the cabinet, and who, I am sure, is proud of his province, has not prevented this slur being cast upon it. The Minister of Railways and Canals

and other ministers from Ontario seem to be afraid to protest against It. It may be that there is truth in the story that an effort is being made to get the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Trade and Commerce out of the cabinet and that therefore these gentlemen are afraid to stand up for Ontario. The Prime Minister has evidently decided that we will have an election this fall, a year before we should have it, and he hopes by thus taking an unfair advantage through these lists to carry six counties.

Mr. Chairman, as seconder of the amendment of the hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) I wish to express my disproval of the course pursued by the leader of the House in introducing legislation to deal especially with Ontario in respect to voters' list. In the last session of the legislature, prior to the election just held, not a word of protest or condemnation of the Whitney administration for their preparation of the voters' lists was presented nor has any complaint been heard since the .election. I have not heard a valid argument advanced why Ontario should be legislated against in this respect. The right hon. gentleman knows that the people of Ontario are anxious for a fair and honest voters' list. His own party had charge of the preparation of these lists for over thirty-six years, and since this party came into power in 1896 elections have been held on the voters' lists prepared by the legislature of that province.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

The Prime Minister says ' hear, hear.' Why is he not now willing to trust himself and his government to a voters' list prepared by a provincial government in Ontario now? There can be but one reason. I do not wish to single out my hon. friend trom Rainy River (Mr. Commee) but my hon. friend has a history in Ontario, he was a prominent follower and supporter of Sir Oliver Mowat in days gone by and continued a support of the Liberal party in the legislature. He has a record that is all his own, peculiarly his own, I do not wish to refer to it, but if the right hon. gentleman had turned a deaf ear to my hon. friend and had asked the honest people of northern Ontario whether they thought federal lists should be prepared for the coming election, I am sure the answer would have been that they were quite satisfied with the lists they had and did not ask the government to go to the expense or to single out that part of Ontario which will soon become an organized district. This course will not bring support to the right hon. gentleman when he appeals for support to the people of that district. I think he could afford to trust the people of Ontario. They applauded him in days gone by, he announced himself prior to 1896 as a champion of provincial rights. That was his great cry in Ontario and other Mr J. D. REID.
provinces and many people in that province,
I think too many, trusted him and voted for him-the right hon. gentleman may smile, he has heard predictions before, but I venture this prediction that when the election comes my right hon. friend will receive from these northern districts a rejoiner such as he never received befoie, because of this Bill. Neither in the discussions in this House nor in the newspapers of Ontario, even the ' Globe,' have any valid reasons been given why the government should not adhere to the policy of provincial voters' lists for federal elections as they did in 1897. Why do they depart from it ? Because a Conservative administration controls affairs in Ontario now; there fore my hon. friend asks for special legislation providing for special lists in northern Ontario in order to give the Liberals a better chance. I am surprised that gentlemen from Ontario on the other side of the House have not protested against this invasion of the rights of that province, they sit quietly and allow this Bill to go through without a protest. The Minister of Customs who is well and favourably known in Ontario, whom the people have honoured, who has called loudly for provincial rights and has told the people of the fairness of the right hon. gentleman and of the government he is supporting, sits quietly by and says : It is all right, we shall have a special voters' list for my own province in the unorganized district. I want to say a word or two to the Minister of Justice. I am sure when at the close of the session the Minister of Justice reflects upon his position he will have cause to regret that he was the father of this Bill which strikes at the province of Ontario. Evidently one reason for the action of the Minister of Justice was that he might save the hon. member for Rainy River, but I venture to think that although that hon. gentleman may put on the voters' lists all the employees of the Grand Trunk Pacific in his constituency, it will not save him at the next election.
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) think that the judges to whom this matter will be entrusted would put on the voters' lists employees of the Grand Trunk Pacific who have no right to be there?

I do not know, and I am not going to speak for the judges. My argument is that the preparation of these voters' lists should be left to the province of Ontario, and the hon. member (Mr. Miller) has supported that principle in the days gone by.
He will support anything.

Of course, he will be compelled to support anything that comes from the government.	.

An bon. MEMBER. He was independent once.

We have not seen any evidence of that since he came to the House. 1 tell the First Minister that he is making a serious mistake when he presses through parliament legislation which is an invasion of the rights of the people of Ontario.

Before the motion is brought to a vote, I desire to add a word to the protest which has been made by my colleagues from Ontario. It is rather a singular thing that nobody finds a word to say in support of this clause. The Prime Minister has no word in support of it; the Minister of Justice is dumb on the question and he cannot hear anything we say ; and the Solicitor General, who ought to be in his place earning his money, is out of the House successively and continuously. I protest, in the first place, against the unfairness of making us discuss a question with a man who cannot hear us and with a sub-otticer who ought to take this legislation, being well paid for his job, out of this House and shirking his proper duty. What use is there in addressing an argument to a man who has got to wait until he reads ' Hansard,' and then maybe to-morrow he will vouchsafe an answer. We could avoid f3hat by having the Solicitor General put in charge of this Bill. But the Prime Minister does not give us either a chance to discuss the matter or to put a man before us who can discuss the matter with us. In that he is unfair to this side of the House, which at least does wish to discuss and put its reasons with reference to these various measures before the government and parliament. Of course, it makes no difference-to men on the other side of the House. They have no criticism to offer ; they are not supposed to offer any ; they are not invited to offer any ; their's is simply to vote whatever the Prime Minister wants, and it makes no difference to them whether the Minister of Justice can hear their arguments or not, or whether or not there is a Solicitor General in his place who can hear. But with us it is a little different, and I protest against this abuse of his position by the Prime Minister. We must not forget the legislation with which the right hon. gentleman came down to this House, on March 9th, and we must not forget the legislation with which he came down some two months after. And we cannot help expresing the opinion that if he had climbed down just a little bit further it would have been better for his own reputation and better for the public life of Canada. He and his Minister of Justice came down with a proposition to invade their old code rig|hts, the provincial control of franchises, in the case of four provinces, three of which are now administered by their opponents and the other of which is still in their grasp.
The Prime Minister, more than any other man, at one period of his career, took tihis simple and logical position:	I
prefer to trust the provinces in the matter of these franchises and in the matter of preparing the voters' lists. The right hon. gentleman went further and said : I will trust these provincial governments, even though they are opposed to me, for although in some cases wrongs may be done, yet upon the whole I believe the virtue of the principle will overweigh occasional wrongs, and even with that in view I argue for provincial franchises and provincial control of the lists. But a change came over my right hon. friend's vision, and this legislation was introduced on the 9th of March ; introduced in all its boldness-so bold that my right hon. friend was himself a little terrified when he came to look at it. lam charitable enough to think that he did not give that legislation thorough personal revision until it had been discussed many days in this House. If I am wrong in that it makes it no better for my right hon. friend. But the bold proposition he came down with was : To seize the making of the lists in the province of British Columbia, from which no single note of dissatisfaction or protest had ever come to him or to any member of his government. Why did he single out that province? For no other reason than that he did not want to single out the province of Manitoba alone, and so, for the sake of company, he added in British Columbia. And when some few of the members from British Columbia gave a tardy and lukewarm submission to the measure, not one of them made a note of strong complaint, and in fact the consensus of their opinion was that both sides of politics believed there were fair and just voters' lists in British Columbia. But he proposed to take hold of the province of Manitoba. He grasped the province ' of Manitoba in 1904 through a subclause in the present election law, and by means of a forced revision, a partial revision, a scandalous revision, in which the thin red line outrage was perpetrated to his knowledge and to the knowledge of his colleagues March 9th, 1908, he proposed if possible to get a legal way of doing what he did before in an illegal manner, and so avoid the judgment of the Supreme Court of Manitoba, which pronounced that the thin red line action was illegal. And so he proposed to put his own partisans in charge of British Columbia, in charge of Manitoba ; men appointed by himself, started in after the writ had issued to do the whole work of enumeration, of notification, of revision and of notification again, in the short period which elapses between the issuing of the writ and the holding of the election. No amount of argument of the Minister of Justice, specious as it is. that they were allowed to do it either before or after the issue of the writ affects the question at all. You must



take the maximum of the power that the government takes in any legislation and criticise it upon that, and the maximum of the power they took was to place their own creatures in charge of this matter after the writs for the election were issued and to do the whole work of notification, and enumeration, and revision, in that short and impossible period of time.
Then, Sir, they took hold of the province of Quebec as to its unorganized districts and of the province of Ontario as to its unorganized districts. That was the intention of the right hon. gentleman and his Minister of Justice ; that is what they proposed to push through ; that is what their following in the west, outside of the British Columbia province, assisted them in attempting to push through, and for which they fought week after week with the strongest of language and the stoutest of backbones, determined to push it through and to teach the Conservatives what they ought to be taught in the province of Manitoba. Well, Sir, something happened. My right hon. friend, began to sense what he was trying to push through, and the fair-minded men in the country began to say that he had gone further than he should have gone, that he had bitten off more than he could chew without injuring his political digestion ; and after a month and a half or two months he came down. He left the province of British Columbia alone ; he left the province of Manitoba alone; he deserted the stalwarts of the province of Manitoba who had made their plaints-one, two, three, four, half a dozen of them, set out in long affidavits and in long statements that they read in the House; what was, according to the Minister of Justice, incontrovertible proof of the terrible wrong that was being done to them. He deserted them all, he climbed down, and he is hanging now by the eye-lids to the little unorganized territories of the province of Ontario. Why did he not drop that, and complete his reputation for being honest and fairminded. Having let all the rest go, why does he hang on to this ? There is the same obloquy, the same unfairness of spirit, the same lack of argument to back it up that there was in the other case. Why did he desert the stalwarts from Manitoba and cling to the one lone man from Rainy River ? How do these gentlemen feel about it ? After all their partisan support, after eating the leek and being dragged through the mire at the heels of my right hon. friend's devious policy in the west, to be sacrificed on the altar of seeming fair play, and yet to have this spotless dove from Rainy River made their particular favourite and put up on high. How do they feel about it ? My right hon. friend has not only to square his accounts with the ' Free Press ' of Winnipeg and with those ardent followers of his from the west, but he has to square the Mr. FOSTER.
account which yet remains with reference to his treatment of the province of Ontario. They will not discuss it here. His followers from Ontario will not open their mouths here. Let me tell him that this discussion has only begun, and that before this year is over there is not a hamlet or town in the province of Ontario that will not hear of this insult to the government of Ontario, and fully heed it. My right hon. friend snaps his fingers in the face of public opinion. Once when I was talking to him across the floor of the House, when I put his pledges of 1896 before him, and his performance of none of them, the right hon. gentleman pulled himself up and said : ' Well, Sir, what are you going to do about it ?-we are here and you are there.' Yes, my right hon. friend is there ; he has his majority behind him, but it is a majority which he got in 1904. Another question is, how the country feels in 1908 ? My right hon. friend is bucking up, without the best backing, against a government which has the very best backing. He, the leader of a moribund and disintegrated government, is bucking up against the Hon. Mr. Whitney and a fresh, vigourous government. He, with a majority in a moribund parliament, elected four years ago, is bucking up against a government in the province of Ontario which has the verdict of the people of a little more than a month ago, and an overwhelming majority in favour of that government-95,000 of a majority in the province of Ontario, formerly his right arm ; and is it because that has been lopped off from his support that he visits with this petty revenge, if I may call it such, with his puny punishment, the province which had refused to recognize his lordship and refuses to bow to his sovereignty ? Well, if he does, he will only find after the next election record is placed on file, that his majority from the province of Ontario will be still less. There are fairminded people amongst the Grits in the province of Ontario. Mr. Whitney's majority of 1904 and his majority of 1908 show that there are more than Tories in the province of Ontario that will vote against a party which has been false to all its pledges in provincial matters, and much more against a party which has been false to all its pledges in federal matters. My right hon. friend has not given a reason. The Minister of Justice has not given a reason. He visits with that superior smile of his any objection which is taken from this side of the House, and deigns no answer. But my right hon. friend and his Minister of Justice have to get out before the people of this country, before the universal trial judges of this country, and have got to answer there for this legislation against the province of Ontario. I ask my right hon. friend whether this was not his position in 1896 ; did he not say : We will take the provincial

franchise and the provincial arrangement of the list ? He did. Did he not say : We hold power in our hands, and If we find that these are violated and gross instances of injustice are shown, we will have a chance to remonstrate with the provincial authorities, and if they do not conform with what we believe to be right, we have then the further right to take the matter into our own hands. That was his position; how has he carried it out ? I ask him to say whether or not he has had the courtesy to communicate with the Hon. J. P. Whitney or the attorney general of Ontario, giving them the grounds on which he thinks wrongs have been done in those constituencies, and asking them to examine into them, and if they find that these wrongs have been perpetrated, then to provide the means for redress.
Such I venture to say he has not. I venture to say that neither he nor his Minister of Justice ever had the courtesy to approach the government of Ontario and put the case before it. Why ? Because they had no case. When a case is to be put, it must be a reasoned one, based upon substantial evidence. But the Minister of Justice takes this absurd and petty position that because the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Con-mee) has said something in this House and read something in this House, both of which he may believe to be true, but which have been absolutely and categorically denied by my hon. friend from West Algoma (Mr. Boyce)-and one member's word is just as good as another's in this House-because that hearsay statement has been made, my right hon. friend and his Minister of Justice take it as evidence upon which they can base this extraordinary piece of legislation. Why, the Minister of Justice gave away the position himself. He said he had heard nothing that could be called evidence and that evidence was the only thing that should guide one. I have no evidence, he said, and without evidence we cannot properly ascertain the true facts of the case and the basis of the difficulty. Yet he has not seen fit to take evidence. Neither has the first minister. The government has not proceeded in that way at all ; but on a mere expression of dissatisfaction, on the mere assertion of one member met by the equally positive denial of another, just as intelligent and just as well posted, he has brought in this Bill. That is all there is, and yet on that evidence, which in a court of law would not hang a cat, which would not be permitted to have the least weight before any judge, our Minister of Justice-save the mark-in this Dominion parliament has thought fit to interfere with the sacred right of the franchise and attack the honesty and administration and good intentions of a local government. What answer has my hon. friend ? There can be none. He has not been courteous nor honest nor fair. What he should have 411}
done, when the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) made the statements he did-what he should have done, if he thought there was a possible case, was to-collect the data, put the case before the Hon. J. P. Whitney, and then if nothing were done, he would have some reason for grasping power which otherwise he has no business to lay a hand upon, and in laying hands upon which he is going against his own principles and his own record.
Then I asked my right hon. friend a question regarding the unorganized districts in the province of Quebec and what reply did I get ? The Minister of Justice replied, and his reply shows the bareness and the baldness of the whole case. He said there were hundreds of people in the unorganized districts in the province of Quebec who could not vote. What does the right hon. gentleman propose to do in their case ? Or is he only looking after those whom he expects to vote for the Grit candidate. Is it not as much the business of the Minister of Justice to see that the hundreds of voters in certain unorganized districts in the province of Quebec are given votes as to see that some voters who, it is alleged, have been left off the lists in the unorganized districts of Ontario, should be put in a position to vote. Is my right hon. friend solicitous that these voters in the unorganized districts in the province of Quebec should be In a position to exercise their franchise? If so, there is just as much imperative necessity that they should be looked after and organized and put in a position to exercise their rights as it is that these voters in the unorganized districts of Ontario should enjoy the franchise. But what has been done ? My right hon. friend has dropped Quebec but hangs on to Ontario. Why has he dropped Quebec ? He gives a very ingenuous reason. He says that the party friends who lead the government in that province may be trusted to make matters right, but in the case of Ontario the hon. Mr. Whitney, just returned by an immense majority, and his government cannot be trusted to do what is right. Why, the right hon. gentleman never asked him, never gave him the opportunity, and up to the 30th of June of this year, Mr. Whitney, both by his declarations and the power he possessed, could have remedied this matter of appeal, if my right hon. friend had deigned to enter into communication with him. Mr. Whitney had the power, the will and the desire, but my right hon. friend seems as anxious to keep a grievance as my hon. friend from Rainy River (Mr. Conmee). Both of them cherish grievances. They can give over the unorganized districts in the province of Quebec to the provincial legislature but they refuse to trust them to the province of Ontario.
The right hon. gentleman has gone too far in this matter, the defect alleged is that there are voters in the unorganized dis-

tricts of Ontario who have been left off the list. But why were they left off ? Because the local elections were held on the 8th of June, and consequent!}' there was not sufficient time to take appeals and have lists revised. But that is a difficulty only for this year, if it be one, and what is the hon. gentleman's proposed legislation ? Does it confine itself to remedying that grievance this year ? No, but the right hon. gentleman makes that pretense to grasp the unorganized districts, eleven of them, for all time to come. His measure goes immeasurably beyond the grievance and proves that it is not a desire to remove a real grievance which animates the right hon. gentleman but a desire to grasp the voters' lists. Take all your newspaper statements and the statements made in the House, and you have only one or two or three places where any grievance is alleged, but you see that as a pretext to grasp the whole eleven unorganized districts. Why do you do that ? Not because you want to remedy a grievance localized in two or three places but because you wish to have the organization of those districts permanently in your hands. That will not appeal to the peonle of Ontario. It will not appeal to fair minded men throughout this Dominion. And after all, take out your partisans on the one side and the other, and you have the salt of the political earth in the shape of that large number of thinking people, growing every day larger, who hold the balance of power and who exercise an independent spirit of criticism and judgment with reference to both political parties. That you are outraging. The public sentiment in this country will not go with you. It will go against you and you feel it has gone against you when you give the people a chance to speak by their ballots.
I protest as strongly as I can. I make my protest here, throughout Ontario and this Dominion : and if these hon. gentlemen will not give a reason for the belief that is in them, they will be obliged to give it when we meet them at the poll.

It is well understood that it is highly desirable no lengthy speeches should be made at this stage of the session, and therefore I suppose many members may keep quiet who otherwise would feel it incumbent on them to take part in the debate.
But It seems to me that hon. members opposite want some one from the province of Ontario to speak on this subject. My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has gone into one of his paroxysms, one of these streaks that at times take possession of him, and has tried to wax indignant about a thing that, it seems to me, can be treated reasonably. What is this fuss about? What is it that he is going to discuss with the electorate?-and that, I suppose, he will give us the privi-Mr. FOSTER.
lege of discussing with him. He tells us that some outrage is being committed, that war is being entered upon against the Whitney government, tie says that we will find that we are up against the Whitney government. We are evidently up against some individuals in this House who hope some time to form a government, my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) being one. It is with them we will have to fight; we are not fighting with Mr. Whitney at all. We are seeking to have our own rights in this matter. We are not departing from our principles-
Oh, oh.
I think hon. gentlemen opposite have admitted that we have kept that one plank in our platform.
You are spoiling it now.

Then do not hon. gentlemen opposite see how wrong they were for years in stating that we had not kept even this one? If they were wrong then they may be wrong now. We are seeking to have the new lists in places where there are no municipally-prepared lists. But 'there are no municipally-prepared lists in the unorganized districts. There was special legislation by the provincial legislature to deal with these unorganized districts and provide for making up the lists. Hon. gentlemen say this Bill is special legislation. We are proposing to do the same thing with reference to Dominion lists. Is there anything wrong in that? The special legislation providing for making the lists for the Ontario House was carried out by partisans. Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Paterson) allow a question? Does he propose to move an amendment to apply this to the province of Prince Edward Island?
I am not proposing any amendments to the Bill. We are discussing this question of Ontario and this alleged outrage of which hon. gentlemen talk.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Paterson) probably did not catch the drift of my question. He said the government proposed to take charge of the making of the lists where lists were not municipally prepared. I supposed, of course, he would move to apply it to the province of Prince Edward Island where the lists are not municipally prepared.
I will do the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) the justice to say that he is not so dense as not to understand what I said. We are discussing Ontario
Why not apply the same to Quebec?

The subject under discussion now is Ontario. According to hon. gentlemen opposite, if we were trying to do this thing in Quebec we would be doing the monstrous thing that they declare we are doing here. Now, whether a monstrous thing or not, we are doing it only in Ontario, and, therefore, the discussion can be confined to Ontario. There was necessarily special legislation by the provincial legislature to provide for the making of these lists for the provincial elections. I maintain the right of this parliament, in perfect consistency with the principles we announced in the past in favour of municipally-prepared lists, to legislate specially for the preparation of lists for the Dominion election. It has been argued by hon. members opposite that this is done for the sake of the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Conmee), that this Bill, if rightly named, would be called : A Bill to elect the present member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River. Of course, they were.

The hon. member (Mr. J. D. Reid) says they were. Now, what is proposed under this Bill? Is it proposed that the government shall appoint its own creatures to prepare lists? Nothing of the kind. May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?
Let me go on

Order. Oh, oh. Sit down.

My hon. friend from North Toronto alluded to that class of citizens who, as he says, are distinct from political parties and who, he claims, are the remnant that save the country, and declares that the people will condemn this Bill. Will the sane and fair element in the community, the people who view questions fom a non-partisan point of view, say that a measure which provides that the judiciary shall prepared the lists is a partisan outrage? Will these men say that the judges will prepare the lists in such a way as to give the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River a seat that he is not entitled to? Is this their estimate of the judges of this country? Can they imagine themselves raised to the judicial bench, and willing, in that lofty position, to act as mere creatures of the government to make a list for the election of men to parliament who could not be elected fairly? Because you have appointed the judges of the land, according to these gentlemen, to prepare the lists, and that task being confided to their hands, they are going so to manipulate these lists that the hon. member for Rainy River and others can be elected when the people don't want them. Will he not be in

a nice position in making that argument on the platform before the people?

No.

there are eighty ridings in Ontario in which you use the lists prepared by the local government, and in the other six ridings you have a special preparation of the lists. There, instead of having the lists made by partisan officers of the local government, we propose to have the lists made for these constituencies by the judges of the land. That is the proposition that goes before the people, that and nothing more; and instead of being an insult to the Whitney government, their lists being right and proper, when the revision of these lists take place, the judicial revision which every man must admit will be honest and fair, and when that confirms the righteousness of the Whitney lists, why, the Whitney government is exalted and we will be cast down, especially the member for Rainy River who does not believe that this is the case. emphatically, so far as we could follow him, that the lists prepared by the officers of the Whitney government and revised by the judges of the land, are fair and honest lists. It has been stated that there is a properly prepared list In the unorganized territory and that no evidence was produced in this House to show that that list was defective, unfair, improperly and illegally prepared and- stuffed. I made assertions on a former occasion that it was an unfair list, that it was illegally prepared, that it took an unfair advantage of one political party, that it was prepared by political partisans, the enumerators being the nominees of the Conservative candidates in the local elections.
Would that be the reason for introducing this Bill ?

No, not the whole reason ; the hon. member himself gave the reason for its introduction ; two years ago he spoke for nearly three hours discussing and showing the imperfections of our present Act in regard to the preparation of lists for Dominion elections. He claimed that gross injustice had been done to him in his riding. He repeated those arguments during the present session, and if a strong case could be made out for a change in the law, he is responsible for making such a case. His whole argument led to that point.
The very provisions that I complained of are continued in this Act.

I entirely differ, they are not. The Act he complained of provided that the lists must be prepared after the writs were issued and the accusation was made against this government that It was a partisan list, hasty and therefore an imperfectly prepared list, and there was a good deal of ground for some of those allegations. It was in view of that that the government, as far as I [DOT]know, undertook this legislation, in order that they might be relieved from allegations of that character. in order that they might have a fair and reasonable list which would be regarded by fair-minded men as just, as between the political parties. Such a list should not be prepared during the heat of a Dominion election, when perhaps men go to greater extremes than they would at other times. These were some of the reasons, if I understood the Prime Minister aright, which justified the introduetoin of this legislation. It was timely and much needed legislation, as the present law is defective. The legislation was brought down before the statements were made by me, but the reasons given, I think, are sufficient to show the necessity for it and they are additional evidence that this legislation is absolutely necessary if we are to have a fair list. Does my hon. friend think that the present Dominion law if acted upon in the same manner as in the past would produce a fair list? He is on record as saying it would not.
What I complained about was the corrupt administration of the law by this government, and my words are ou record.

And what I am complaining about is the corrupt, partisan, and fraudulent administration of the provincial law. he was instructed by telegraph to hand all papers and money to Mr. Donald Hogarth. In the first place when I was accusing the enumerators of being partisan and of pre-pa ling lists without any notice and stealing a mean advantage over their opponents, the hon. gentleman from Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Boyce) was quick to jump to his feet and contradict that statement because he said that he knew Mr. Ashforth would not be guilty of such a thing. Well that is correct. Marie (Mr. Boyce) will admit that there is no more capable man in the country than Mr. Ashforth. No such statement has been made and no such statement is true if it is made.
It is on ' Hansard.'

My. hon. friend is wrong. It is on ' Hansard,' there was a mistake as to the name and that might have misled the gentlemen at Toronto for a short time, but nobody claimed it mislead Mr. Ashforth, so far as I remember, who told me himself he was appointed enumerator.
When ?

Last February ; and the document read by the leader of the opposition is proof that he had no instructions. He was referred to Mr. Langworthy for advice and instructions and he never got them Why did not he get them ? I leave hon. gentlemen to answer that question for themselves. He did not get them because he was not the kind of man they wanted. Let me illustrate that by another instance. We hear a good deal from gentlemen opposite

about the virtue and righteousness of the Whitney government and their officials and their administration. I have never attacked that administration and its record and I do not think it is a fair thing to do ; and I am going to make the remarks which I feel called upon to make now because the name of a respected citizen has been attacked in this document read by the leader of the opposition. Mr. Ashforth was a member of their license board and it was proved up to the hilt that two members of the board were bribed and had received money. An investigation was called for and a gentleman came up to hold the investigation and when he got to Port Arthur he found there was something in the rumours, and where do you think he held the investigation? In a back room 7 feet by 6 feet of Mr. Garrick's office. Two or three bold spirits found their wav in there and the commissioner was just about to close his books as there was no evidence. when they called on him to subpoena Mr. Downing and Mr. Downing's evidence disclosed that he gave $400 to one member of the board and $200 to another. The man who got the $200 admitted it ; the gentleman who got the $400 did not deny it but lie said it was given for another purpose. The hon. gentleman is entirely wrong. What does the hon. gentleman know about it anyway ? This affidavit says positively he never visited that section.
And the man who went there swears he did.

The original of this affidavit was filed with Judge Yalin at North Bay and the date is omitted from this copy.
I think we could get the original if necessary.

Yes.

I do not know whether he passed on it or not. The enumerator never went up into that district to make lists.
It is like the affidavit read by tile member for Winnipeg

When the friends of the Liberal party appealed to Mr. Hugh to have the names of men who were well known to be qualified placed on the list he said he would receive no names in that way, although they were supported by affidavits, and that these men would have to appear before the judge. That would mean a loss of four days and there are not many voters who would lose that time to go before a judge in support of an appeal. That kind of thing was done throughout the whole district. In another case a notice was posted on a school house that the enumerator would be there at a certain hour on a certain date, but it did not say what territory would be embraced, and a number of voters appeared for miles round and they were told by the school teacher that nothing was known about the enumerator except what was posted on the door. After waiting for two or three hours they went home, but the enumerator came later on and made up a numerous list supplied by one or two of his friends who happened to be there.
What place was that ?

North of New Liskeard, in Nipissing.
-Mr. BOYCE. That does not give us much information.

Here is a letter X received from a very prominent citizen of Nipissing and this is what he says with regard to the lists :
The lists in this riding are a disgrace. In some oases the lists have been changed after the enumerators court was held. In McPherson and Kirkpa/trick the names put on at the enumerator's court were afterwards left off the list, thereby disfranchising a large number of Liberal voters. About forty were left off in McPherson and Kirkpatrick, and thirty in Hugel, and the same thing occurred all through the unorganized townships. I am getting a large number of charges prepared and will be able to prove scores of cases of corrupt practices.
These names were not placed on the list and the enumerators kept them off. The enumerator was E. A. Wright who holds a dozen positions under the present government, and I think he is under suspension at present for some wrong-doing in connection with the license board, he being chairman of the license board of the district of Sturgeon Falls.
That shows the Whitney government punishes wrong-doing.

The name of the writer of the letter is Mr. H. E. McKee of Sturgeon Falls, barrister.
Some hon. MEMjBERS. Oh.
Yes, and he is as reputable a man as there is in this House or out of it, that is who he is.
We saw him down here the other day.

I can give you another and the hon. member, for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Boyce) will probably find some fault witb this man because nothing is right in the eyes of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyce) unless it emenates from one of his own peculiar friends. This letter says :
In New Ontario the Liberal candidates can attribute their defeat to two things, viz.:
.1. Voters' lists prepared by enumerators who did not display even the slightest degree of fairness. Liberal voters in large numbers were left off lists, while many Conservatives were placed on lists although there was not any qualification possessed to entitle their names being added to lists. Foreigners in large numbers were placed on lists and they voted for Shillington, the Conservative candidate. Here in the town of New Liskeard, Wing Deer (a Chinaman) who is not a naturalized subject voted for the Conservative candidate. Let me say just how these names were collected. The police magistrate, the road inspector, the homestead inspector, the Crown lands agents, division court, clerk, division court bailiff, license inspector and in fact every government official collected the names of Conservative voters for enumerators.
Lists were carelessly made up. In on9 poll here there was a case of one elector voting twice. The Christian names of two electors were E. and E. R. and the same individual voted at two different times in the same poll. Instead of posting lists as required by Act. some enumerators kept them locked up in safe so our men could not have access to them.
To accept such lists for Dominion election purpose? would be utter nonsense. Why it would mean defeat before the campaign started.
Hon. gentlemen opposite boast of the majority of the Whitney government. I can tell them that if it were not for stuffed lists in Temiscamingue, Nipissing, Sturgeon Falls and Sudbury, Mr. Whitney would have four supporters less than he has today.
Is thatr an affidavit which the hon. gentleman has just read?

No, it is not necessarily an affidavit. Hou. gentlemen opposite are 412
as hard to please as the enumerators in that district. They want an affidavit to place any Liberal voter on the list, but any old name handed in by a Tory heeler goes on me list at once. I wish to call your attention to the state in which cur voters' lists are in this district. Robert Jamieson, livery owner; Henry Yar-kie, livery owner; Thos. Inglis, livery owner; Thos. Barret, butcher; W. Whelan, teamster; P. Savord, boarding house; Geo. Vaillaneourt, boarding house; Joe Milway, restaurant; J. Milkie, pool room; W. Searson, baggage man; Fred. Deacon, clerk ; S. Fielding, carpenter ; Joe Beaudry, labourer ; D. Rouileau, restaurant ; R. Robertson, labourer; W. Klntrea, clerk; W. Lett, clerk; Thos. Code, clerk; Arthur Deschaut, labourer; R. Bruyere, labourer.
I can't just remember all of the names, but there are several more, and that is only in the little town here. All through the country it is the same way.

Here is something from another portion <TC the district:
Warren, Ontario, June 15, 1908. Mr. C. A. McCool, M.P.
Seeing the approach of the federal election, I will take the liberty to notify you about the voters' lists which has been used for the provincial election in this distriot of Sturgeon Falls. It has been so tampered with that quite a few names have been taken out of it. People who have been voting for some forty years '(Liberals) are missing. I consider it to be my duty to post you and the other members on these facts. Hoping to be of service, I remain truly yours,

Here is another case from the Temagami district :
In Temagami and vicinity about 100 Indians voted. They were all sworn, but took the oaths in Harley township. The poll was not opened until a quarter to ten o'clock, and some of onr good friends left and came to town thinking it was not going to be opened. We have cases in which men had their fare paid and in which men voted under other men's names. When you consider that the government officials in this district, including the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway employees, amount to about 600, and the way the province went in general, what can you expect?
With regard to the Indian vote, I may say that these Indians are wards of the

government who receive their annual treaty money. At the last election X venture to say that the same trick was played at Temagami that was played at Haileybury in 1890. The Indians were on the list by virtue of the revising barrister, and three men did duty for forty voters in the town of Haileybury. I venture to say that the same thing happened at Temagami, because you could not otherwise get the Indian vote at that time of the year. I venture to say that not more than half a dozen were present. A particular friend of the party opposite has since boasted to me how he did the trick ; he took the Indians each time and redressed them and got them to go and vote. The men who do such things are rewarded by the local government. I have here the ' Haileyburian,' which ought to be sufficiently Conservative to carry weight even with the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie, and in it there is a letter from Williams Hugh to his friend Mr. Farr, which reads as follows :
Englehart, Ontario, July 6, 1908.
Dear Mr. Fairr,-The Hon. Frank- has, through the department, directed me to open a land office at MoDougall chute-now Mathe-son.
This is a news item, you will of course put this in your own peculiar way. I regard Mr. Cochrane's action in transferring me as approving my efforts in the settlement of this district, which you have done so much to bring to the notice of the landless.
Yours truly,
Mr. Cochrane approved of Mr. Hugh's election work.
When your reputation is as good as Mr. Cochrane's, it will be a good deal better than it is now.

I do not have to go to the hon. member for East Simeoe to get a reputation in this House dr out of it. While Mr. Cochrane is an old friend of mine, he is no angel with wings any more than is the hon. member for East Simeoe. The hon. member for North Toronto repeated what he said were the words of the premier, that occasional injustice with regard to the lists by zealous friends might be overlooked. I say the same thing. But the matter is different when it affects a whole district from one end to the other. The district of .Nipissing is not all unorganized.
I think only about one-third, or 7,000 or 8,000 voters are in the unorganized section. There might be an occasional slip on the part of the enumerator, an occasional leaving off of names, but when the thing Is done from one end of the district to the other, it is high time the government should step in and do something to protect the lists. I am not surprised at hon. gentlemen opposite wanting to hold on to these lists, 1 Mr. McCOOL.
for they know just as well as I do .what was done in the last election.
W'hat was done ?

I will tell you what was done in one case to my own knowledge, in the hon. gentleman's district. We have a number of men working up there in our lumber camps at Searchmount. Out of 150 men, only one man was singled out to be put on the list, and that was because the bush rangers informed the enumerator that he could be counted on to vote Tory. Just one man out of 150. It is all very well to say that these lists can be appealed, but unless the voters really entitled to vote are placed on the list in the first place, it is almost impossible to get them on later because, in the majority of cases, they have to go ten, twenty or forty miles to be registered. How many voters can afford to lose two or three days' time in order to go and register ? Is it expected that the candidate will bear that expense ? Why, it would cost thousands of dollars. All we ask is a fair list, a list prepared, as this Bill calls for, by enumerators appointed by a bench of three judges. We make no complaint whatever about the municipal lists, but on the other lists it is not possible for us to have .a fair election. I therefore trust that the amendment will carry.

If there is any man who has a little to complain of in connection with the lists, it is the hon. member for Nipissing, and right well does he know it. There is not a list made up in that district as he well knows, which was not criticised in the making and which was not the subject of- appeal, or in respect of which there was not an opportunity for appeal. The hon. gentleman has nlaced himself in a very invidious position-in exactly the same position as the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Bole) did with regard to the Manitoba lists. Did he use that declaration where it would do any good ? Yes, he took it to the district judge. He or his minions took some evidence before the district judge on an appeal from the very same list, and having heard that he had some declarations, I made inquiries from reputable counsel, who was present at that court, and that gentleman said that these affidavits were laid before the court and the judge did not believe one word of them.
Where did the hon. gentleman sret that information ?
Yet the hon. gentleman has no hesitation in coming to this parliament and reading copies of declarations which were repudiated by the court of record on which he tried to foist it.
Will the hon. gentleman

I will not be interrupted. My hon. friend would not answer me a

question wittr regard to tne authorship of his document and I refuse to allow him to interrupt. Forsooth there Is the evidence upon which this great high and mighty .Minister of Justice based his Bill. Here is the declaration and the evidence, which I presume he could not use because it was labelled with the cloak of privacy. There stands this great Minister of Justice who said that this Bill was rendered necessary by reason of certain information-some of it in letters and some of It on oath-referring to the district of Nipissing. But when asked to produce that evidence, he was ashamed to do so. But he can get it through another avenue and that is the avenue of the hon. member for Nipissing, who has no shame or scruples in endeavouring to lead the House to believe affidavits which the Judge repudiated. When the hon. member for Nipissing tried to make the House believe that the enumerator had refused to go to portions of the district where there was a population and where it was his duty to go, he merely repeated what his master, the Minister of Justice, said. The Minister of Justice said that the enumerator in Nipissing did refuse to go to a district where he should have gone and where there was a large number of Liberal voters. Has there been a word to substantiate that ? The enumerator is bound by the Act, and the hon. member for Nipissing knew well that neither the enumerators in the district of Nipissing or in any other district declined to go to every place where they were required by law to go. That the enumerator in Nipissing did go to every place and district set down correctly all entitled to be on the list and wilfully omitted none is absolutely proved by the affidavit of the enumerator himself. Surely that should avail against a declaration repudiated and rejected by the district judge. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that there is not one place in that district he was required to visit to which he did not go.
That is not true.

Then the converse must be the case, and my hon. friend must assert that, of his own knowledge, there were places where it was the enumerator's duty to go and where he refrained from going. Will he state what places they were ?
Yes, at the junction of the Temiskamingue and Northern Ontario Uailway with the Transcontinental Railway.

Will my hon. friend tell me whether that was a polling place? I am asking for information. The hon. gentleman has made some serious charges. He said that, according to his own knowledge, this enumerator had refused to go, or bad refrained from going, to a place to make an enumeration where, by law, it was his duty to go. Is that correct ?
I do not know that I catch what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyce) is saying.
I am talking at the top of my voice.
I understood him to ask if there was a polling place at the junction of the Temiscamingue and Northern Ontario Railway and the Transcontinental. How could there be when there was no list ?

Then my hon. friend (Mr. McCool) is lamentably displaying his absolute ignorance of the law when he states that, to his own knowledge, an enumerator refused to go to a place where, by law, he was required to go. The hon. gentleman made that statement, and he displays his ignorance of the Act in making the charges in this wild and reckless manner. Section 60 of the Act says :
The enumerator shall visit every part of the territory where by the statute or by proclamation of the Lieutenant Governor in Council there is required to be a polling place.
What was that enumerator to do? The Ontario government had not appointed a polling place, and he would have been derelict in his duty had he gone where there was no polling place. Let the hon. gentleman place the responsibility where it should be placed ; let him go to the Ontario government and ask why a polling place was not established there, and he will get his answer from the very gentleman whose name be has reviled, Hon. Frank Cochrane, than whom there is no more honest or more capable administrator in the government of the province of Ontario. And I say it ill-becomes my hon. friend from Nipissing to revile the name of the Hon. Mr. Cochrane or to cast a slur upon him in this House. He dare not do it in the presence of or in the hearing of Mr. Cochrane. But I, for one, will take good care that the hon. gentleman's words and mine are conveyed to that hon. gentleman.
I rise to a question of privilege. The hon. member (Mr. Boyce) is putting words in my mouth that I never uttered. I never said a word against Mr. Cochrane.
Oh, oh. '
I did not say a word about him at all until his name was interjected here by the hon. member for Simcoe, except to read a letter in a newspaper.

I am putting my construction, for which I am responsible, on what the hon. gentleman said concerning Hon. Frank Cochrane. Was there a protest entered against the election in Nipissing? The time for it has gone by. Is the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCool) going to be like the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Bole)? These

hon. gentlemen make charges of Chinamen voting, aliens voting, and all voting Conservative. How he knows which way their votes are cast I do not know, for there are no numbers on the ballots now, thanks to tlie Whitney government. The hon. gentleman makes these complaints here, but where these claims would be pertinent and proper, in the courts in Nipissing or Thunder Bay and Rainy River, they are not heard of. My hon. friend from Nipissing cannot point to a protest in a court of law to show that the election was attacked there.
It is not too late yet.

Then I put it to the hon. gentleman : If he has the public interest at heart, and if anybody besides himself !s enough interested in these grave offences to come forward and present the protest, let him go on and claim justice. But for nearly two hours hon. gentlemen on that side of the House have detained this committee and kept back the progress of this Bill by retailing statements on hearsay about matters concerning which they have little or no personal knowledge. The hon. member for Nipissing did pledge his personal knowledge to one statement, but it now turns out absolutely without a shadow of justification; and the hon. gentleman stands In the Invidious position of not only taking up the time of this House, but of stating facts which he knew had been repudiated where they were pertinent, trying to drag them in here after they were repudiated where the facts are best known.
