House in committee on Bill (No. 115) to amend the Dominion Elections Act.-Mr. Aylesworth.
On section 1,

The expression used by the right hon. leader of the government in the earliest stage of this Bill with reference to the character of the lists which are to be produced under this Bill, namely, that they were to be made entirely on judicial authority, is altogether incorrect. One would hardly believe that the government would be disposed to descend to the practice of the deceit involved in that expression. To the extent that appeals are made from the lists as prepared by enumerators under this Bill, the lists will be prepared under judicial authority. The judges will hear and dispose of such appeals as are made, but only in case either party sees fit to appeal. Apart from that, the only connection which any judge will have with any list produced
129S5

under this Bill, will be that he will appoint the enumerators. Except for that relation with these lists, the judges will never see any of them, and have no connection with them whatever. That expression has been used, apparently and necessarily, with the intent of producing in the minds of those to whom the expression is addressed, the belief that the other lists, that is, the lists produced under the provincial Act, are not the work of the judges, and that the judges have no part, lot or interest in the preparation of those later lists. The right hon. gentleman himself in using that expression, was doubtless well aware of these facts. The Minister of Customs this afternoon, who dwelt at great length on the same subject, and played upon the same string, is perfectly aware, and the press supporting the government throughout the country who have rung the changes upon that expression ever since the Bill was introduced, are perfectly well aware that the self same judges who, if there are appeals, will deal with appeals under this Bill, and with the lists produced under this Bill. These self same judges are the judges who in the past, have produced, and in future will continue to produce the lists under the provincial Act. The self same judges sitting in the same building will perform the same functions with regard to the lists which are made under this Act as they have always performed, and now perform, with regard to the provincial lists produced under Mr. Whitney's legislation, in fact, under the legislation which obtained in that regard before Mr. Whitney's government came into power. It is to be hoped therefore that no one will be deceived by being told that the lists under this Act differ in any respects as regards their judicial origin, or any part the judges may have in their preparation, from the lists which are at present produced by the same process under the provincial Act.
Now, with regard to this section 1, I wish to make a few observations, and I invite the attention of the right hon. gentleman to the points which I propose to raise. In paragraph 9 of section 1 power is taken to judge of the time of the year when this revision shall be made, and new lists made under this Act. The time of the year when these lists are made should be the same in every year, that is, In every year when the power "of suspension is not exercised. The provincial Act does not contain such a clause as this, allowing the government to order lists to be made any time and every time thev see fit, they are made at a particular time of the year, the enumerators are to begin their work not later than July and thereafter the procedure goes on as provided under the Act. In subclause 1 of 9a the government have taken power to make theses list* at any time, not limiting themselves to the months of July. August or September mentioned in the former part of of the subsection.
With regard to subsection 2, the committee will observe that we are to have for the production of these lists in the unorganized territory a board of registration composed of the various district court judges. It has not been explained why such an innovation is necessary, why there should be a Board of Registration in unorganized Ontario while the County Court judge, each in his own county, in all other parts of that province, performs the entire function of revising the lists in organized Ontario. I subrnh there is no necessity for forming this Board of Registration, but that each district judge in his own county is quite as competent as the county judge in his county throughout the rest of the province to do the necessary work under this Bill if it becomes law. It has been suggested and probably with a great deal of force, as this Act has been styled an Act for the relief of the hon. member for Thunder Bay, that this innovation is introduced for his benefit; because he is not satisfied to have the district judge in his own district act in reference to the list in that district, but desires that some person else should be called in to assist. Under section 57 of the Ontario Voters' List Act the judge does the work, and 1 see no necessity for the formation of a board of registration. The more reasonable course and the course consistent with uniformity would have been to have adopted the provisions of the provincial law with regard to the making of these lists and that the work of the enumerators in making their enumeration should have been conformable to the provincial law, not that these enumerators should go on and do their work of enumeration subject to the supervision and according to the directions of the Board of Registration. Surely it is preferable that the work of enumeration should be laid down in the statute and not be left to the dictum of a board of registration or of a judge. The. enumeration is much more likely to be made in a uniform and proper manner, the same in each district, if it is done under a statute than if it is done under the direction and supervision, as laid down in subsection 4, of a board of registration or of a judge.
McCarthy. In what respect does the hon. gentleman refer to this ?

Subsection 4 says :
4. Such board of registration shall appoint for its electoral district as many enumerators as are necessary, and it shall be the duty of such enumerators, under the supervision and in accordance with the directions of such board of registration, to prepare the voters' lists for those parts of the province without municipal organization in such electoral district.
The Ontario Voters' List Act lays down a procedure for the enumerators to follow. They are, within a certain .time, to issue

notices that they will be at certain places at certain future times and will there make up the enumeration and place upon the list those entitled .to go on. I think it would have been better to have followed that procedure in this statute rather than place the enumerators under the supervision of a Board of Registration. The effect of allowing this to be done, according to subsection 4, will be to produce a result which will not be uniform in the various districts.
With regard to subsection 5, it is provided that the provincial law is to be observed as far as possible.
McCarthy. Will not that govern as to procedure?

It will probably govern just as far as the judges and enumerators see fit to observe it, but if any difficulty arises the likelihood is that it will not be observed. The statements of the hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) with regard to the lists made up in his electoral district in 1904 show the manner in which the same provision, which was in the law under which that list was made, was laid aside.
There was no variation from the provincial law in my riding in 1904.

If the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) is prepared to make that statement after listening to the facts given in minute details by the member for West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) I am satisfied that he should take that position.
The hon. member gave details of the preparation of the lists in his own riding, but you referred to my riding and there it was not the case.
The same order in council regulated the procedure in all unorganized districts.

I do not care when the order in council was issued, the procedure in the district of Thunder Bay and Rainy River was right, under the provincial Act. That can be verified and there was no fault in the Rainy River district.

I desire to call attention to paragraph 5 of 9a which provides that:
5. In the preparation of such lists the provisions of the law of the province regulating the preparation and manner of revising and bringing into force the provincial voters' lists in the like oases shall, as far as possible, be observed and followed, but the revision of the said lists shall be had before the board of registration, who shall hear all appeals from the said enumerators, and no person whose name is not included in the voters' lists so prepared and revised shall be entitled to vote.
It appears to me that provision will be in direct conflict with section 13 of this

Bill. Section 13 provides for the case of voters' lists in overlapping polling divisions and that any person whose name is on the general list, but by mistake has been dropped from the separate list, may, on taking a certain oath, vote. The provision here is that no person * whose name is not included on the voters' list so prepared and revised ' shall be entitled to vote. Further than that, section 11 of the Dominion Elections Act deals with the several classes of persons who are entitled to vote in Dominion elections although their names are not upon the provincial list. There is nothing to ensure that the persons named in section 11 will be upon the Dominion list to be produced under this Bill. The section of the Provincial Act enumerates the persons who shall not vote, giving a long list, including provincial officials.
Does the hon. gentleman contend that section 11 of Ihe Dominion Elections Act is affected by this legislation ?
It may be.
Do you really think it is ?
Yes.
Where and how ?

I am proceeding to show. Section 12 of the Provincial Elections Act contains a list of persons who shall not vote, for example; Judges, customs officers, clerks of the peace, county crown attorneys, certain postmasters, certain stipendiary magistrates and certain inland revenue officers. It is quite within the range of probability that some if not all of these may be omitted from the lists prepared under this Bill. Although they are not on the provincial lists yet they are good voters by virtue of section 11 of the Dominion Act, and section 150 of the same Act which provides that although they are not on the list yet by taking a certain oath they, may be allowed to vote. It may very well happen that some or all of the persons disqualified by the provincial Act will not be on the list prepared under this Bill. The latter part of subclause 5 provides :	That no
person who is not on the voters' lists so prepared and revised shall be entitled to vote. There should be a provision introduced into this clause to the effect that it shall except those provided for under section 13 of this Bill, and also under sections 11 and 150 of the Dominion Elections Act Otherwise the general effect will be that' there will be two entirely inconsistent clauses in the same Act, one making a person a good voter and another declaring he had no vote. It would also have saved a great deal of work and expense If the Minister of Justice had adhered to his original proposal
129)89

to make the provincial lists the basis of the new lists to be prepared under this Bill. Under the clause he originally proposed the enumerators would have taken the provincial lists in force and have added the necessary names, and the judge would have stricken out such names as should not be on the list.
Is not that the practical result anyway when you have these provincial lists before you ?

The judge does not make the list and it would be quite within the power of the enumerator to discard the provincial lists entirely under this clause as now drafted. Then, under subsection 6 of the Bill it is provided that when the judge has completed the list the enumerator has to transmit a certified copy to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery and to him alone, whereas under the provincial Act certified copies of the list are to be deposited in the office of the clerk of the peace, of the stipendiary magistrate, of the sheriff, and of the police magistrate. Under this Bill copies of the lists are deposited only at Ottawa and not in the electoral district affected. I think copies should be deposited in the same offices as are provided for under the provincial Act. Clause 1 provides that the judges have power to divide the whole province of Manitoba and the unorganized districts of New Ontario into new polling divisions ; and that they may. also make distinct and new polling divisions every time they make a Dominion list. I believe there is no necessity for the judges either in Manitoba or New Ontario altering the polling divisions in any respect except where overlapping takes place, and I think that was the agreement arrived at.

It seems to me that the amendment of the Minister of Justice providing a definite period for the preparation of the lists, obviates the necessity for the last words in section 1 which read : Or be had during other months of any year. The Ontario Act provides a definite period in the year during which these lists are to be made, namely, that the enumerator shall start to prepare the lists on or after the first day of June and not later than the first day of July, and the very essence of the Bill is to provide that the time should be made as definite as possible for the making up of these voters' lists. If we have a definite period for the preparation of these lists, as suggested by the Minister of Justice, between the 1st of August and the loth of October, why enlarge that or run the risk of enlarging it, and make it absolutely indefinite by adding the words, ' or be had during other months of any year.' If the lists could not be made up betweeen those dates, they might be made up in the depth of winter. I therefore move that the section be amended by striking out these words.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Those words were not inserted without purpose. It might be impracticable to conduct the preparation of the lists during the specified months. No one can tell what might happen. There might be an unexpected by-election taking place in the mouth of June or in any other month of the year in any riding in respect of which it might be important that the lists should be modern, or should not be of an age they would otherwise have if we were compelled always to rely on the last lists prepared. In these circumstances that is a latitude which can do no possible harm. There would be no object, unless there were a necessity, of having a revision of the lists oftener than once in the year, and there is power in the Governor in Council by proclamation to dispense altogether with the preparation of the lists in any year when such a preparation seems to be entirely unnecessary.

There does not seem to be any provision for the publication of the proclamation. I would move that the words, 1 to be published forthwith in the Canada Gazette,' be inserted after the word ' proclamation ' in the tenth line.
Amendment agreed to, and subsection 1 as amended agreed to.

It has been already suggested by my hon. friend from Prince Edward (Mr. Alcorn) that this work of preparation, revision, and so forth, should be confided to each judge for his own district; otherwise in so enormous a territory there will be a great deal of confusion. I do not know whether the government have taken that into consideration, but it seems to me that there is a great deal of force in what the hon. gentleman has urged.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is a practical difficulty about the working out of any such suggestion as the hon. gentleman has made, and it was only after considering the difficulties that it seemed to me it was much better that there should be a board consisting of more than one judge, as the Bill proposes. There are six constituencies in question. I think there is not one of them in which there is not a greater number of voters voting upon ordinary municipally-prepared or ordinary manhood suffrage lists than will be voting under the provisions of this statute. Perhaps I am wrong in thinking that in every constituency it will be less than one-half of the whole number of voters to whom this statute will be applied. But there is none of the six constituencies with regard to which this Bill will have universal application ; and I think that in the greater number of those six constituencies, there is more than one district judge having jurisdiction. You

do not want to single out in an Act of parliament an individual judge by name ; you do not want to say either the junior or the senior ; you cannot do better than, adopting the language I have selected, make the senior judge, who has jurisdiction in any part of the territory, ex officio chairman, so to speak, or one at all events of the board, and let him select his colleagues from his neighbours. The only possible objection is, that it will be slightly more expensive, but that as an objection is offset by the manifold advantages. X am not sure of the exact number but I think there are, counting the two new district courts in these six constituencies, eleven district judges. Then there are to be six boards of three formed out of those eleven judges. Surely in that way, seeing that some of those judges will be on more than one board, it will be better to have a board of some sort, acting by its full body or its majority, than that each judge should be responsible for the work in his own district. These are very large districts, there would be in many cases a tremendous extent of territory which it would be necessary for a judge to cover, but this would be the best practical way of working it out.

I do not know whether the minister has considered the position in which these judges will find themselves at this period of the year. Take the electoral district of Thunder Bay and Rainy River, tiiere will be three judges in that district having territorial jurisdiction, none of whom will go outside the district of Thunder Bay and Rainy River.
There are not three judges at present.
There will be.
Yes, in all probability.

The senior judge will be Judge Chappel of Rainy River. Suppose he chose for his board Judge Johnston of the Soo and Judge O'Leary of Port Arthur. It will be seen that, both for the purpose of appointing enumerators and the consideration of appeals, Judge Johnston would be taken away froin the Soo and Judge O'Leary or Judge Chappel taken away from either Port Arthur or Kenora for a considerable time. That is not all. During that period another judge will be taken away from Manitoulin for instance. A judge might be taken from Sudbury into the eastern part of the district. Great confusion would result, and just at the time when judges are required for the revision of the organized municipal lists. From the 1st of August to the 15th of October is the period during which the municipal lists in the organized portions of the district are being revised. Why create all this confusion when, at this time and in conjunction with his own duties, the district judge, revising Mr. AYLESWORTH.
the lists in his territory, could himself revise the lists in the ordinary way without calling in two judges away from the performance of their judicial duties. I really suggest that the assigning to the judge in each district the appointment of an enumerator ip the territory within his jurisdiction and giving him, under this Act for the purposes of revision, the same power as under the Ontario Act, would save expense and a great deal of inconvenience and confusion.

The idea of a board of judges is not mine, but I can see many advantages in it. We are trying to get a fair list. It is generally admitted that a board of three judges is more likely to be fair. Does my hon. friend think that Judge Chappel does not know the whole of the districts of ;Thunder Bay and Rainy River ?
Each judge would exercise jurisdiction where he does know everybody, and the gentlemen he would call to his assistance would be strangers who in reality could only render him formal assistance.

I do not understand it that way. This is different from revising the lists. These judges now conduct the preparation.of the lists, they allot the polling places, appoint enumerators, issue instructions to the enumerators regarding their conduct and the preparation of the lists by them. That is far different from revising the list after it is prepared. They will do that also.
Who will be best fitted to judge the enumerators-the judge of the district or two outside judges t
The Bill gives the judge the selection from the judges nearest to him.
He must take strange judges.

He must in the case of my riding. Judge Johnston is far more familiar with Thunder Bay district than Judge Chappel. There are many other reasons why a board of judges would be much preferable. We are very proud of our judiciary and I think we have the best system of any country ; but judges are human after all, and the principle acted on by this and previous governments is that it is better, when appointing a judge, to take a lawyer away from the district where he practises. It is better that the judge should be away from those who were his clients when he was practising at the bar, and there are social and family considerations and others which make it more reasonable perhaps to have a board of judges than a single judge.

But the cases are not parallel. It has been suggested by my

hon. friend from West Algoma that the judge should know personally the enumerators lie appoints. That is a very different question from deciding cases. Of course, he is called upon to decide questions between strangers ; but, in appointing men to positions' of trust, he should appoint those whom he knows.

It is not merely the appointment of the enumerators, but the general procedure in the preparation of the lists. The provincial law governs that to a great extent. This board of judges must give instructions and these instructions should come from a disinterested body. The complaint against the present provincial lists is that they have been prepared by partisans, that the instructions were given purposely to take advantage of the opposite political party. I did not suggest the idea, but I can see a good deal of fairness in it.

The hon. member's local knowledge is much better than my own. In the district of Thunder Bay and Rainy River where there are three judicial districts, would it not be better to have three judges meet and formulate their scheme for enumerators and have the same system for each judicial district ? The only possible argument against it would be, not one of fairness, but of the little initial expense. It seems to me that the scheme formulated would give uniformity in the constituency. First get the judges together, and you will have uniformity of instructions to the enumerators, and, as the result of that, you will have uniformity of decisions afterwards on points raised before the board.
What about the selection of enumerators ?
McCarthy. They are suggested by the three judges.
Would not one who knows them make a better selection than three, two of whom do not know them ?
But the board as a whole would yield, no doubt, to the suggestions of each member concerning his own district. And, by having the three judges you would have fairness and uniformity of decision.

There are two reasons against it. The hon. gentleman wiil see that the time allowed for making up the lists is, comparatively speaking, short. The hon. member for Thunder Bay complained of this. You have now from August 15 to October 15. What are you going to do when you are cornering up all the judges ?
They appoint the enumerators.

Yes. but instead of having three judges working in one district, he
could have the three working in their several districts, and each carrying on this work in connection with his regular district duties. Again, would it be better to allow the judge to attend to his judicial duties and the work assigned him in the place where he exercises jurisdiction, or would it be better to take him away from his district at a time when, it may be, his district court sessions are being held or he is revising municipal lists, and give him work elsewhere, clogging the judicial machinery, not only by taking the judge away from his own work but by making slower the work that is 'assigned to him ? Would it not be better, instead of having three judges, to have each judge work in his own territory where he has knowledge of the conditions and of the people ?

I do not agree with the hon. member (Mr. Boyce). I think this will expedite matters. The three judges meet only for the purpose of selecting the enumerators, formulating the rules and fixing tlie polling places.
What about appeals ?
They come before the judges In the ordinary way.
They come before the board of judges.

Not necessarily.
Mi*. BOYCE. That is what the Act says.

Yes, the hon. gentleman is right. I had not quite realized that point. But I am glad of it. This is tantamount to an election trial. Formerly the provincial law provided that an election trial might be held before one judge. That seemed unfair and now the law provides for two judges. The board of three judges will deal with these matters better.

If the government are disposed to insist upon a board of registration which will probably be unworkable, they will have to take the responsibility of it. Having made our protest and shown that this Bill will be, in our opinion, unworkable, I do not know that wre can do any more. That it will be unworkable must be plain to hon. gentlemen who heard the discussion this afternoon. The hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. McCool) declared that the process of appeal could not be carried out effectively because, he said the population is too scattered and the judges too far away. If with one judge sitting, it is impossible to give an effective judicial revision you can imagine what the result will be when you require the attendance of three judges to hear every appeal. The case need only be stated to see the consequences. However, we have made our protest. I believe the provision will be unworkable. But the government insist, upon it, so let it pass in that form.

The government should remember that Judge MeCurry is an elderly gentleman and it is not reasonable to expect him to go out of his own district. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) must know that.
On subsection 4,
i- Such board of registration shall appoint for its electoral district as many enumerators as are necessary, and it shall be the duty of such enumerators, under the supervision and in accordance with the directions of such board of registration, to prepare the voters' lists for those parts of the province without municipal organization in such electoral district, and the Governor in Council may confer upon each enumerator so appointed any powers necessary for the discharge of his duties.

This will be subject to the same objection as has been pointed out by other hon. gentlemen with respect to subsection 3. Apparently, it is designed to make this procedure as cumbrous and unworkable as possible. I do not know whether there is any ulterior motive behind it. Some of my hon. friends think it is designed for the purpose of postponing these elections on the ground that the lists cannot be prepared in time.
That is it.

I am not suggesting that as my own idea, but I know that some hon. members on this side are impressed with it. There is not the slightest doubt that if the present provincial system ir liable to delay, and is found to be practicably unworkable as has been alleged this afternoon, the system now proposed of three judges will be much more unworkable. I do not know that we can say anything about it. if the government insists upon absurdities of this kind, it is only necessary to remind my hon. friends on this side of the House that they could not possibly listen to any greater absurdities than those which were alleged this afternoon as a basis for proceeding with the Bill at all. Therefore, inasmuch as the Bill is founded on the most grotesque absurdity that could be imagined, it seems eminently proper that every provision should be of an equal absurdity. ,

Not the least absurdity of the procedure will be the very simple question as to the right of a man to the franchise, a question which will come up over and over again in the courts, will have to be decided upon by three judges, as if it were not possible for any person of ordinary intelligence, having an ordinary acquaintance with tlie right of franchise, to decide such questions for himself.

I want to say this to the right hon. gentleman and to the Minister of Justice, that having lived in that country for twenty-four years, and having in view Mr R. L. BORDEN.
the provisions of subsection 1 of this Bill, and knowing the conditions which exist in that country, I can only say to him that it will be absolutely impossible to get those lists made up within the time the Minister of Justice has fixed therefor, and to have anything like a reasonable time for the preparation or revision of those lists. The thing is physically and absolutely impossible.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not in a position to judge of my hon. friend's statements. He gives me one version, and my hon. friend behind me gives me another version. Which one shall T accept ? The matter has been carefully looked into, and I am advised that the Bill can be worked.

Take the case of the district of Muskoka. In that large riding there are only three or four townships that are unorganized, and what will be the result if the lists are not completed ? You disfranchise a splendid riding for the sake of two or turee townships where there is only a handful of votes. You say under the Act that you may go outside the district for judges. Every person in that country knows that Judge McCarry, of Parry Sound, is a very old gentleman, and I do not believe that he would leave his home in Parry Sound and go down a number of miles to the district of Muskoka to take a hand in these three or four scattered polls. Where are you going to get another judge ? The next nearest judge will be at Kenora, or else Sault Ste. Marie. But the senior judge of Sault Ste. Marie will be at Thunder Bay.
North Bay will he closer than that.

The judge at North Bay will be occupied in the Nipissing district. If the lists are not completed in Parry Sound, you are disfranchising a splendid, well settled riding, all because perhaps thirty or forty voters who reside in the organized districts have not been placed in the lists in their polling divisions.

I suppose there will be not less than thirty polling subdivisions where the lists are prepared in the district of Rainy River. I think there might be as many as that. Then there are .thirty polling subdivisions in which the board of judges has to sit for revision.
They do not have to sit at every polling subdivision.

They have got to sit somewhere in that riding, they have got to appoint days for hearing appeals in .these thirty subdivisions. The probabilities are that there will be appeals in each, we must contemplate appeals in each one of the thirty subdivisions. Then, under this, law, the senior judge at Port Arthur chooses the senior judge in my district, Judge Johnston

and off he goes to Port Arthur on a revising trip. If he takes two appeal courts a day, it would take him fifteen days to complete the tour ; if he takes one a day, he is away thirty days. Now that is only one instance. But that'is done with regard to six ridings, and there is where the confusion is involved, and there is where the Act is unworkable. In the first place, you have not only got to contemplate one set of three judges and the inconvenience that will exist In their territory by their absence, but you have to contemplate more than that. Take this territory between Thunder Bay and Algoma. You have to contemplate that Judge Johnston may be designated by the judge of Port Arthur, and that Judge Johnston later on may be chosen by Judge McCallum, or by Judge Valin in Nipissing. Supposing that Nipis-sing has thirty to fifty polls, and you only have sixty days for the notice, for the appointment of enumerators, for the enumeration, for the notice of appeal, for the appeal itself, for commencing the lists, sixty days, covering a territory twice as large as the settled portion of the province of Ontario.

McCarthy. I think the hon. gentleman's fears are unfounded. I am acquainted with the district of Nipissing as well as the hon. gentleman. He supposes that there are thirty polling subdivisions, but it is not for a moment to be supposed that the board is going to sit In every polling subdivision. They will divide the territory into districts. In my own riding, a township with twelve subdivisions, the judge only sits at one place in the whole township. Take the whole county of Simcoe. Last year the voters' lists in that whole county were revised by one judge, although the county has a population of 70,000 or 80,000. So I do not think the fears of the hon. gentleman are well founded.
What are the distances there ?

The distances are not as great as yours, I admit. But the mode of travel is very rapid. The hon. gentleman suggests fifteen or thirty sittings in one district, or one constituency. I do not think that would be necessary at all.
Does my hon. friend know the country? Take the polls along the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific and you get there in a day.

McCarthy. The hon. gentleman makes a false assumption that the judges will sit in every polling division. They will form districts and sit at central points. The difficulties are not as formidable as he presumes, but I suppose they will be greater than in the more densely settled portions. It will not take three judges any longer to get to these various places than it will one.
The Act provides that they shall follow the procedure under the Ontario Act, and that has been that the judge sits for appeal in every place where the enumerator sits.

My hon. friend is perhaps borrowing a little trouble. He asked if the judges would not have to hold their courts along the line of the National Transcontinental Railway. It does not follow that there are any courts along the National Transcontinental Railway. He is assuming that there will be an appeal in every place where the enumerator sat.
It is a fair assumption.

It is not. There will not be appeals in half the places. Court may lie held in two or three places in Thunder Bay, three or four places in Rainy River and the same number in Nipissing. Outside of these districts the difficulties will be very small. About two . and a half months are allowed for the preparation of the lists.
I have not heard the hon. member state his objections to having the judges exercise jurisdiction in the territory over which they preside.
I do not want a judge hearing an election trial.

Now we are getting at it. The hon. member says that the judge who revises the lists in the cities and towns in his riding well and satisfactorily would not be a satisfactory officer to revise the lists in the unorganized territory.
I did not say anything of the kind.

That is the hon. gentleman's position. The. principle is that this should be consonant with the Ontario Voters' Lists Act, and to introduce any other procedure is to render it complicated, unworkable and highly expensive. What are the judges to do with their courts while they are doing this work?
There are junior judges.
There are none in your district.

The judges have to make the voters' lists anyway.
On subsection 5,	.
In the preparation of such lists the provisions of the law of the province regulating the preparation and manner of revising and bringing into force the provincial voters' lists in the like cases shall, as far as possible, be observed and followed, but the revision of the said lists shall be had before the board of registration, who shall hear all appeals from the said enumerators, and no person whose name is not included in the voters' lists so prepared and revised shall be entitled to vote.

I wish to refer to subsection 5 by way of comparison with subsection 3 of the Bill as originally introduced. This subsection is practically the same as subsection 2 of the original Bill. Subsection 2 was followed, and it seems to me this should be followed by a provision of this character-X am quoting now from subsection 3 of the original Bill :
3. In the preparation of such lists the voters' lists which were prepared for the several polling divisions situate wholly or in part within the electoral district or wholly or in part within such unorganized territory as such polling divisions were established at the last preceding provincial election, and which under the laws of the province, are then or were last in force for the purposes of provincial elections, shall be taken . . . and the names of all persons who are not qualified to vote in the said electoral district shall be struck off the said lists, and the names of all persons qualified to vote in the said electoral district and not already on the said lists shall b9 added to the said lists.
Why is that omitted? It seems to be a proper provision, having regard to the scheme of the Bill in the first instance. Even in the Dominion Franchise Act, as the hon. gentleman will remember, the basis was to be the municipal lists, and the hon. gentleman thought it was strange they were not strictly adhered to. But then, although they were not adhered to, they were taken as a basis ; we took such provincial lists as were available and adopted them as a basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The clause which we have in the Bill as reprinted is drawn upon a different footing altogether from the clause in the Bill which was originally introduced. As I explained when I moved the second reading of this Bill, to my mind the clause I originally framed was a perfectly fair clause. Taking the Ontario Voters' Lists Act as an example, if the Ontario Voters' Lists Act is a fair measure, providing, as it does, for the preparation of the lists in the unorganized territory by men appointed as enumerators and selected for the work by the Ontario government, I am absolutely unable to understand why that same measure ceases to be a fair measure and becomes an utterly partisan, nefarious, iniquitous, monstrous and wicked scheme, when the very same thing is done by the Ottawa government instead of being done by the Toronto government. Either both of these methods of preparing the lists are entirely partisan or unfair, or each of them is an equally fair way of preparing lists for the purposes of an election. Adopting the principle that whatever the government In power in any province or any parliament did was fair, I prepared the original clause upon the footing that the enumerators should be appointed in accordance with the provisions of whatever the provincial law was, and starting with these Mr. l. g. McCarthy.
provincial lists as a basis, that they should prepare the lists upon which the Dominion elections should be carried out. That was objected to very vehemently, and it was said on the other side of the House and accepted upon this, that to be absolutely fair we sjiould depart altogether from the system of government enumeration or of government appointment of enumerators and have judicially appointed enumerators and so have lists that were perfectly impartial and perfectly pure. Upon that footing I prepared this clause and I ignored altogether the partial-and impure if you like -lists prepared by partisan enumerators and started the judicial enumerators upon their work of preparing their lists from the ground up. I think that is a consistent position, and I have drawn this clause in order that these enumerators acting under judicial direction, upon judicial appointment, with judicial supervision from first to last, and subject to judicial control, shall prepare lists which shall be fair to each party and with regard to which no one will have ground for any complaint.

If the Minister of Justice would give us a little less rhetoric and a little more information he would do something to facilitate the progress of the Bill. I pointed out that even in the Dominion Franchise Act which these gentlemen opposite railed against, you always took the provincial municipal lists as a basis and that was the provision in this Bill when first introduced. The Minister of Justice seems_to have no idea about this matter except the idea of party or partisanship. I was not discussing it from the standpoint of partisanship; I was discussing it from the standpoint of the rights of the people whose names are on the provincial lists to have their names remain there unless some good reason is shown for taking them off. That seems to be an intelligible principle, but apparently it does not penetrate the mind of the Minister of Justice. There is no possible reason for departing from the original scheme of the Bill in that respect. However, I have placed my views before the House and if the government without any reason whatever see fit to insist that the voters iu these northern ridings whose names are on the provincial lists without any question or complaint, shall be put to the inconvenience and trouble of seeing that their names are put on these new lists, the government will have to take the responsibility of imposing that burden upon them.

If the government do not see fit to adopt the provincial lists as the basis for the first list, surely there can be no objection to taking the first Dominion list as the basis for all subsequent lists.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The Minister of Justice who has given a good deal

of attention to this, has come to the conclusion that he wants to have the lists prepared by the iudges from the bottom up, and I do not know that there is much objection to that. Of course any man appointed by the judge will want all the information he can possibly have before him in preparing the lists.
The lists are prepared by the enumerators and not by the judges.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is all the difference in the world between the enumerators being appointed by political machinery or by judicial machinery.
On section 0,
I have heard many absurd reasons given on the other side of the House for this legislation, but I have heard no reason whatever given for departing from the provincial polling divisions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I suppose the judges will accept the local polling divisions which are generally known to the people unless there is good reason to alter them. However, in new districts they may have to be changed from time to time as settlement and population increases, and they certainly should have power to change the polling divisions under such circumstances.

Section 24 of the Dominion Elections Act provides that the polling divisions shall be those provided under the laws of the province for the purpose of a provincial election, the only exception being where the polling divisions are intersected by the boundary between two electoral districts.
Under this Bill new polling divisions may be constituted for each successive Dominion election. I do not see why judges should be empowered to change them except where there is overlapping.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In the unorganized territory, the lists are prepared by a system of registration and the Ontario statute provides that the name of each voter is to be entered in that part of the voters' lists the polling place for which is most convenient for him. Is it to be the enumerator or the judre who shall decide that? I should think that the better authority would be the judge.

The question is not about the allotment of voters in particular polls, but about the changing of polling divisions by the judges where there is no overlapping. Why should the judges interfere with provincial polling divisions except where there is overlapping?

That difficulty has been met in the past in the province by the Lieutenant Governor in Council fixing the polling places. There never was an election
in which new polling places had not to be provided. Under the Dominion law the Governor in Council would do the same. If we are taking the matter out of politics, would it not be better to take that out of politics also ?

That is not the point. The boundaries of the polling subdivisions are under the Dominion Act to be those provided by the provinces ; but under this Act they may, as my hon. friend from Prince Edward (Mr. Alcorn) says, be sub-divided differently for each election, so that it will be a case of confusion worse confounded at each election, respecting the place where a man will vote. With regard to section 7, why not, use the provincial lists if they are more recent ?
Section 7 has been considered and passed.

The hon. gentleman, who is speaking for the Minister of Justice, says section 7 is passed. We are in this position, that we have a deaf Minister of Justice, who listens to his own side of the House, and turns a deaf ear towards this side. When there is any objection raised on this side of the House, the hon. gentleman takes advantage of his infirmity and will not listen. I do not think there is anything worse for any country to suffer from than a deaf Minister of Justice.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman should withdraw the expression ' taking advantage of his infirmity.'

If that be out of order, I will certainly withdraw it ; but I say that this House lias suffered from it, especially during this debate, and the country has suffered, and the country will resent it, and will lay it to the charge of the right hon. gentleman who persists in retaining that minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think I will accept that responsibility without any hesitation whatever.

I was proceeding, when I was interrupted by the hon. gentleman who is assuming the functions of Minister of Justice, to ask why this government sees fit. where there is a provincial list prepared regularly and not more than three months old, and where there is a Dominion list eleven months old, to declare that you shall have the Dominion list, and that the people cannot vote upon the provincial list, which is more recent. It seems to be a proposition that would shock the common sense of most people, especially in view of the pronouncement of the right hon. gentleman that these provincial lists must be accepted as the lists upon which the Dominion elections shall take place. One of the excuses of the Minister of Justice for this

legislation is that he wants fresh lists ; and in the case 1 have mentioned you are going to prefer a stale list and are going thereby to disfranchise all the voters who come into a constituency in the meantime. They cannot get on the list and the right hon. gentleman proposes to leave them disfranchised.
McCarthy. Surely the hon. gentleman who has been prattling this whole afternoon has got this into his head at last. Not content with continually prattling-
Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The word ' prattling ' is not in order.

McCarthy. I withdraw the word ' prattling.' The hon. gentleman who has been continually and volubly speechifying on this Bill all this afternoon, and not content with this continuance of his volubility, which but for your ruling I would continue to call prattling, does not understand the first principle of the Bill; he now tries to insult the ministers of the Crown. The hon. gentleman has followed the example of the hon. member for North Toronto, who made similar insinuations this afternoon, but no attention was paid to them. Such insinuations are not worthy of this House ; they are certainly beneath the dignity of members of the House of Commons. Surely if a man be ill and while ill is prepared to sit in this House and do his duty to the country, it ill becomes these hon. gentlemen to allude to the fact as they have done to-day. The man who seeks to make sueh arguments is beneath the dignity of manhood, in my judgment.
I must again rise to order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the expression ' beneath the dignity of manhood ' should be withdrawn.
I will withdraw the expression, and if there were another word that I could substitute for it, within the parliamentary rule, I would adopt it.
I protest again, and I will continue to protest as often as the hon. gentleman makes these remarks.

McCarthy. I have withdrawn the expression. As to section 7 of this Bill, the hon. gentleman asks again, why not use the provincial lists ? This whole Bill is based on the assumption that we will not accent the provincial lists, for reasons given in this House this afternoon ; and when we have passed the clauses providing for the necessary machinery, why reiterate what has already been said ? Now that this wise Solon has spoken, this independent gentleman Mr. BOYCE.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When the Bill was in committee before I stated that I would prepare an amendment which would make it an offence on the part of any deputy returning officer to attempt to mark a ballot so as to identify a voter. I propose to accomplish that purpose by inserting a provision in section 20 which amends section 255 of the principal Act, to make the deputy returning officer punishable, without the alternative of a fine, by an imprisonment 4134
of not less than one year and not more than five years, who places on any ballot paper except as authorized by this Act any writing, number or mark with the intent that the voter to whom such ballot paper is to be or has been given may be identified thereby. That will cover the case of marking the ballot paper either before it is handed to the voter or after the voter has voted and returned the ballot paper to the deputy for deposit in the box.

When this matter was up before the hon. leader of the opposition suggested that the onus should be on the deputy returning officer who had the custody of the paper to show that he was guiltless. That is not usual, but in a case of this kind I think it is right. The deputy returning officer has the custody of these ballot papers and it ought not to be possible, if he has ordinary intelligence and is an honest man, that this thing could happen.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is possible unfortunately.

McCarthy. There is this difficulty. John Smith might have some vindictive feeling against the returning officer and might put a mark on the ballot himself in order that the deputy might be convicted of a criminal offence. The deputy cannot know that John Smith put a mark on the paper because he cannot unfold it, and it would be very unfair to put the onus of proof on him that he did not put the mark on the ballot, when be is the only one who could have marked it, if John Smith's denial be accepted.

What I suggested has not very much to do with what has been just discussed. The discussion has related to the question of determining whether or not the deputy returning officer put the mark

on .the ballot. But that is entirely a question of evidence, and I do not propose to interfere with that in any way. In the absence of proof to the contrary, it should be presumed that the mark was put on the ballot for the purpose of identification by the deputy returning officer, and the amendment I suggest relates solely to the intent and not to the proof that the deputy actually made the mark. I propose that the amendment of the Minister of Justice should be altered so that if the deputy returning officer should place on the ballot paper, except as authorized by this Act, any writing, number or mark, the intent that the voter may be identified thereby, shall be presumed in the absence of proof to the contrary. This leaves it open to the deputy returning officer to prove that he had no such intent, but such intent would be presumed in the absence of proof to the contrary. The deputy returning officer should have sufficient intelligence to know that if he puts any mark on the ballot, the ballot may be identified thereby, but he would be given the opportunity to prove that he had no such intent in doing what he did.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend from Lincoln said a moment ago that any honest man with common intelligence could not make such a mistake as to put a mark on the ballot unless with the intention of finding out for whom the voter cast it. At his particular poll he put his initials on every ballot, and at that poll there was a majority in favour of his political friend. He was an honest man, as far as I know, and an intelligent man also, but evidently had not given the close attention he should to his duties, and he has been lamenting ever since what he did.
What he claimed was that he thought it was the right thing to do because it had been done under the provincial Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He had probably beeif accustomed to act as deputy returning officer in the local elections in which the ballots were numbered, and he did the very same thing in the Dominion election. But .take the case of St. Hyacinthe. Our Quebec law is the same as the Dominion, yet the returning officer put his initials and numbers on all the ballots in his particular poll. He is an honest and an intelligent man, yet he made that mistake.
What reason did he give ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not know that he gave any but he did it without malice. The only objection I have is that Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
to make a man liable to prosecution for having committed such an error, is a very serious punishment. Not only that but you put on him also the onus of proving his own innocence. I thought at one time that we might impose a slight penalty on the deputy returning officer in the ease of every ballot he thus marked so as to punish him for his negligence, if not for his malice, but on the whole I do not think we can do much better than accept the amendment proposed by my hon. colleague the Minister of Justice.

The great difficulty is the little care taken in the appointment of deputy returning officers. They are generally strong party men and very much occupied with the election. The night before polling, they are generally up late, and, instead of studying the law and preparing to do their duty, they are canvassing all day for the candidates of their choice. They go into the poll without knowing the law. And, in the St. Hyacinthe case, the man did not know what he was doing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Possibly.

If ignorance of the law were proved there could be no fraudulent or criminal intent. Therefore, all those returning officers to whom the hon. gentleman has alluded would be discharged by any judge before whom they were brought. Of course, this does not add anything to the risk of prosecution ; they would be subject to the risk of prosecution in any case under this section. The section merely provides that the man shall be presumed to know the consequences of his own act. We should have returning officers who will be sufficiently diligent to make themselves acquainted with the law. I admit that the penalty is severe, but I think we might try this for a year and see how it works.
Would the hon. gentleman suggest that the man should be held guilty before he is proven guilty ?
No. But if he puts a mark on a ballot by which a voter can be identified, it will be presumed, in the absence of some reasonable excuse
That he is guilty ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Putting on the mark constitutes the offence.

He is not held to be guilty, because it remains to be determined whether he can discharge himself of the burden the statute puts upon him. That is not an unreasonable burden. He is acting for the people of the whole polling division or the whole riding. If he violates the law which has been placed in his hand for his information, by putting a mark which would lead to the identification of a voter, the duty is put upon him of giving

a reason why he marked that ballot. That is the whole effect of my amendment.

(a)	which have not been supplied by him; or

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Show it to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth).

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With regard to the question whether the intent to do wrong ought or ought not to be presumed in tbe absence of proof to the contrary, it would strike me as a pretty serious proposition. We are dealing with not less than ten thousand deputy returning officers all over the country. They are men presumably wishing to do their duty ; but they are confronted, when they take charge of their work on election day, with a statute containing some hundreds of clauses which they are supposed to familiarize themselves with and by which they are instructed in a very great number of sections as to exactly what they must do under different circumstances. ' It would he a marvellous thiug if they did not occasionally make mistakes. I suppose that we all agree that where it is an innocent and honest mistake of which we have seen repeated instances in recent times, the man ought not to be punished by the infliction of such a serious penalty as this we have provided. But there might he circumstances under which it might he very difficult for him to prove his innocence. I instanced, the other day when this clause was under discussion, the case of a possible discussion at a poll witli regard to some particular voter-such
things, in practice, frequently occur. A man comes in whose right to vote is questioned, and some wiseacre suggests that the man's ballot ought to he endorsed with a memorandum so that if it turns out that he had no right to vote his ballot can be found and rejected. Now, if, pursuant to that arrangement made by consent of all parties at the poll the deputy returning officer were to write upon the ballot, if you like, ' This is John Smith's ballot,' that would manifestly be a writing upon the ballot for the purpose of identifying John Smith. But I would think that the deputy returning officer ought not to he punished if he did that honestly.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It may be said that he could readily prove his innocence.
I do not know that he could do it so readily. If indicted for this offence, he could go into the witness box and assert his honesty, but whether his assertion will be believed or disbelieved is another story. What you are proposing to do by this amendment is to put the burden of proving himself innocent upon the man who is accused of this particular offence. That is a very serious departure from the ordinary principles of the law. This clause is framed to make it an offence for the deputy returning officer to put upon any ballot paper a mark calculated to identify the voter with intent that the voter shall thereby he identified. The intent is the gist of the whole offence. If the intent is absent the charge falls to the ground. If it is a mark put on inadvertently, of course nobody is to be prosecuted. If it is not done with intent to identify the voter, there ought to be no prosecution. If it is done with intent to identify the voter, that intent may be honest, although in most cases I think it would be dishonest. But to prove dishonest intent, to prove intent to commit the offence struck at by the statute, it seems to me is a thing which ought to be upon the prosecution. Ordinarily it may be the surrounding circumstances Avill suffice to satisfy the jury of wrongful intent. But if they do not, if the surrounding circumstances as disclosed in the evidence leave the jury in doubt, ought we then to say that a man should be presumed guilty unless he is able to satisfy the jury or the judge that he was acting honestly ? I think not. I think we are going the full length when we penalize the man who does this with wrongful intent, and leave that intent to he established by the prosecution, just as it is established in other criminal cases.

Take the case of one man shooting another. If he points a revolver at him and pulls the trigger, he Is presumed to have intended to shoot the other man. The deputy returning officer ought to be in tbe same position. He actually commits an overt act, he puts a mark upon the ballot which he ought not to put

there. Is it not fair to assume that he did it with that intent? Why should not the, onus of proving that he had not that intent be upon mm? When the deputy returning officer places his mark he actually commits an act which he cannot commit legally, and it ought to be assumed that he would know that it would have the result of identifying that ballot.

Gr. McCarthy. Whatever the presumption of the law Is, it would still be the same under the amendment of the Minister of Justice. The leader of the opposition proposes to make that presumption go one step further than the law does. The man who places a mark on the ballot is presumed to have done it with intent, just as the man who presents a gun. I would suggest that if you prove that the man did mark this ballot you have nearly proven your case, and the intent will be presumed. But the onus of proof will be shifted.

If I am not mistaken, both the Customs Act and the Inland Revenue Act furnish many cases where the burden is put upon the defendant of proving that he had no intention of .defrauding the revenue laws. That is done in the public interest. It is necesary that the public revenue should be protected. The facts are peculiarly within the knowledge of the man who is accused. This is a case in which we have something quite as>
important as the protection to the revenue, that is, the protection of the secrecy of the ballot. The deputy returning officer has the law placed in his hands weeks before hand, and if lie sees tit to put a mark of identification upon the ballot, it is not imposing a serious burden upon him to ask that he shall show some good reason to the court why he contravened the law in that way, and in the absence of some good reason, it should be held that he put it there for the purpose of identification.

It is a question whether the court would not infer, by reason of the fact that the returning officer had placed a mark upon the ballot paper, that he had done so wrongfully, because he did it in contravention of the statute. I think the amendment of the leader of the opposition is a matter of surplusage. Any judge would think that a man who commits an act in infraction of a statute did it with wrongful intent. It might appear in the course of the prosecution that the intent would be rebutted by the circumstances, that is, any possible inference that might be drawn by reason of the fact that the mark was on the ballot would be rebutted. But I want to point out to the leader of the opposition that an infraction of the revenue laws is not quite similar to an infraction of the election law. This election law deals with an act which cau only be
committed once in every four years, whereas violations of the revenue laws may take place every day.
Where is the difference?
Ninety-nine out a hundred deputy returning officers are perfectly honest, and if one is guilty by inadvertence he ought not to be put into the position of disproving his guilt.

We want to stop
these marks from being put on by deputy returning officers.
With intent.

We want to stop
them being put on if they have the effect of identifying the voters. If a returning officer does put such a mark on a ballot, we do him the justice of saying that he must do it with wicked intent. But what we are at is not the intent of the man so much as to prevent the voter from being identified, by making it a criminal offence. Of course, it is only fair that it should only be made a criminal offence when the man does it with a wicked intent.

The amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) simply means that in the absence of a satisfactory explanation by the deputy returning officer he shall be presumed to have intended the consequences of his act. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. E. M. Macdonald) said that it would be unfair that the judge should be allowed to draw an inference of innocence from the circumstances surrounding the act.
Mr. E, M. MACDONALD. Not that, but that he should be prevented from drawing an inference from the facts and circumstances appearing.

If the facts and circumstances appearing show or tend to show that the man did not do it with wrong intent, he would be free and the judge would be bound to tell the jury that these circumstances appeared; but if it is clear that he did mark the ballot and that thereby he did identify the voter and marked it with that intention, then he must stand the consequences.	1

If a deputy is charged with having marked the ballot, then at the preliminary examination the magistrate would have no discretion but would have to send the man for trial, because if the amendment of the leader of the opposition carries, the magistrate would have to assume intent to commit a wrong and not having the right to sift the evidence would be bound to send him up, whereas if it is left open and the magistrate is allowed to judge, the whole thing could be cleared up.

If the magistrate had power to try the case he would have the same power to deal with any case as an ordinary trial judge. To say that if a deputy returning officer places on any ballot paper, except as authorized by the Act, any writing number or mark with intent to identify the voter, it shall render him liable to a penalty, is absolutely idle if you do not follow it with the provision that it shall be presumed he did it with that intent until the contrary appears.
I know of no reason why witnesses should not be called in the first instance before the magistrate.

The hon. gentleman must know that if a question of fact is raised before the magistrate and there is any evidence on which to justify the conclusion of guilt, the magistrate has no jurisdiction only to send the man for trial.
The Criminal Code says he must hear witnesses.
It has been held he must send him up for trial.
Held by whom ?
By Judge Gregory of Nova Scotia.

There is no reason why witnesses should not be called so far as I am aware. The observations of the hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick seem to be very much beside the mark. We have many similar provisions in the Customs and Inland Revenue Acts. Take this section of the Customs Act:
Any person, who, without lawful excuse, proof of which shall ibe on the person accused, sends or brings into Canada or has in his possession, any bill-head otr other paper purporting to be a bill-head or blank capable of being used as an invoice



shall be subject to a very severe penalty. There you put the burden of proof on a man in respect of a very ordinary transaction. It is not prohibited by law to have a bill-head in your possession but if he has it brought in from abroad the burden of proof is on him to show that it is not in his possession for a fraudulent purpose. Then section 204, a most comprehensive section, imposes the burden of proof under every possible condition and in every possible variety of suit or proceeding upon the man who may be accused of smuggling or of some infraction of the. Customs Act. It seems to me we would be going no further here but would be acting along the same line of policy in the public interest. The rights of the person charged in every such case are sufficiently protected by the right given to him to bring forward every circumstance to show there was no criminal intent in his mind when he committed the particular act complained of.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not argue that there is not a good deal to be said in favour of the view advocated by the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). I have given a good deal of thought myself to this subject, and I thought at the time some punishment should be inflicted on the returning officer who puts any mark upon a ballot quite innocently, without malice, simply as a punishment for his negligence. I call my hon. friend's attention to the Bill as drafted. First of all the offence is created which is quite proper. But look at the penalty, it is not a fine but it is penitentiary, one of the highest penalties the law can inflict. When the offence is of such a nature and of such consequence it seems to me that, as he has to stand his trial, if he is innocent he is already punished sufficiently for his negligence, and I do not think under such circumstances you should put upon him the further burden of proving his own innocence.

I have listened to many finely drawn arguments as to what the judges and the juries of the country think of any infraction of clause 17, and I have come to the conclusion that there is only one remedy to apply in disposing of this clause. The right hon. gentleman says there were about 10,000 officers in an election carrying out the law, comparatively few of these men are lawyers, and it would not be surprising if here and there mistakes should be made. Some thirty years ago I was acting for the registrar who was returning officer, and I went through the county appointing deputy returning officers and I made it a point to instruct every deputy carefully as to his duty. In the recent provincial election in Halton 1 advised the returning officer to take that course and I believe that in every instance he spent an hour with each deputy returning officer carefully instructing him in his duties. The work was well performed and nothing occurred that in any way tended to void the election. I think we might include in this law a clause making it incumbent on every returning officer to instruct his deputies carefully, more particularly with regard to the more technical particulars, and if such were done we would not have a repetition of what occurred in the county of Wentworth, or many years ago in the county of Hastings where in one case at least the election had to be set aside.
For many years in Ontario we had been cursed with the marked ballot. Working men were coerced by their employers to vote as the employers wanted. I have myself seen a voters' list that was marked from the ballots that were returned to the city of Toronto. Every man's name was marked exactly as he voted, and in a bye-election during the same year on the same list, that list was used in the village where I lived and the electors were coerced by

means of it. We had a marked ballot for thirty years in Ontario, a ballot worse than open voting. We cannot tolerate for a moment any such thing being introduced into the Dominion election law ; we protest strongly against anything that will tend to make the vote of any elector known to his fellows. There is no question in my mind but that by means of this clause 17 the vote of the elector can be known. Suppose it is not made known that would not be the worst feature of it. The bad feature of this clause is, that the employer can go to his workmen and say : This is not a secret ballot, and we will know how you vote and every man can be coerced. The only means of giving us a fair and square election law' is to expunge that clause from the Bill and without taking up any more time I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Blain : That section 17 be stricken out.

McCarthy. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) has misconceived the meaning of section 17. It is in no sense intended to create what w'as called in Ontario the numbered ballot and which did exist previous to the advent of the present administration.

It validates any ballots that may be numbered by the returning officer.
zance of it and would count the ballots. In the Ontario Election Act the verbiage of the clause relating to this matter is practically the same in effect as paragraph 17 of this Bill. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) reflects w'hat teriffic power he would place in the hands of the deputy returning officer who w'anted to act improperly, without this saving clause in the Bill, I believe 11 e will come to the conclusion that the provision is a wise one. It is to the advantage of the party in power that that should be so if they want to do anything dishonest; but it is not fair, and the law should make fairness its aim ; and if you place such a provision in the Election Act as exists in both the Ontario Act and this Act, you will do w'hat is fair and right and prevent the deputy returning officer defeating the intention of an elector.

Ever since confederation we have got along pretty well w'ith the ballot which we have at the present time, and I think we can leave that as it is without opening the door in the wav proposed by section 17.
I do not think the question has been raised more than three times since confederation ; but this section is inserted in the Act for the purpose of preventing it being raised.
Ill that sense it does not. Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) tell me if he is content W'ith the Ontario Election Act as it at present exists ?

I am only satisfied with the secret ballot.
Mr, E. G. MCCARTHY. Have you not contended that the present election law of Ontario gives an absolutely secret ballot ?
I say that w'hat I want is a secret ballot. If this clause is in the Ontario election law I wrant it struck out there too.

McCarthy. That statement may be useful hereafter, but if the hon. gentleman refleets for a minute I believe he w'ill come to the conclusion that this is a fair law. Does he realize what pow'er the present law places in a deputy returning officer w'ho w'ants to do something that is not proper ? Does he not know that it absolutely places in those who hare control of the machinery unlimited pow'er to void ballots. In the county of Wentworth in the last Dominion election because the deputy returning officer put a number on the ballots the local judge threw' out one poll and changed the whole result of the election. I am glad to say the judge in the county of Simcoe did not follow' that ruling, but held that If these numbers were put there with fraudulent intent it w'ould come up properly on a protest; that he could not take cogni-Mr. HENDERSON.
Amendment of Mr. Henderson negatived : Yreas, 22 ; nays, 57

The hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol), who has been obliged to leave the chamber, has asked me to impress upon the House what he suggested in regard to assisting the deputy returning officer not to make the mistake of marking the ballot; and I would urge on the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice w'hat seems to me to be the wisdom of adopting the suggestion, by adding to the section these W'ords : ' but any deputy returning officer placing anv mark thereon shall be subject to the provisions of section 255.' The only thing that can be said against that is that it is a repetition ; but the virtue _of it is that by section 255 w'e are providing that that shall be a criminal offence, and the result of making this addition, although it is not absolutely necessary to carry out the law', will be to reduce to a minimum the probability of a deputy returning officer doing what w'e w'ant to prevent him doing. His attention will be drawn to the matter, because he will read it tin connection with his duties at the close of the poll.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member for Centre Toronto saw me with reference to this suggestion, but I pointed out that this section 173, w'hich section 17 is amending, is a directory section, directing what should be done after the closing of the poll in counting the ballot papers, and it

does not seem to me that there would be any propriety in tacking on to such a section a statement that a deputy returning officer would be subject to a penalty provided in another section of the Act. We have provided for the penalties in one clause and for the directions in another clause in another part of the Act.
He is sure to see section 173 in order to learn what his duties are, while he is unlikely to see section 155 if he is an honest man not expecting to be penalized.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is not at all
likely that a deputy returning officer will turn up section 173 the first thing in the morning, as he has no occasion to use it until the polls are closed in the evening, when it is too late to warn him. It would be much more to the purpose to attach this rider to one of the earlier sections. But he will read the whole statute and try to understand it. I do not think this is necessary in any way. We do rot spread all over the statute-book finger posts at every section pointing to this, that or the other penalty. The penalties are there, and he must read and inform himself in that regard.

There may be some force in what the minister observes, though I would have preferred to have the whole penalties at the end of section 173. At least my hon. friend should undertake in his instructions, to draw the particular attention of the returning officers to the penalties and that would perhaps answer the purpose.

speechtext:
I will undertake to draw the special attention of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to them, but I do not want to undertake a responsibility I may not be able to discharge.

speechtext:

If a voter fraudulently takes a ballot paper tut of the polling station or fraudulently delivers to the deputy returning officer to be put into the ballot box any other paper than the ballot paper given him by the deputy returning officer, he wall fee disqualified from voting at any election for eight years thereafter and be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years and not less than one year, with or without hard labour.

speechtext:

speechtext:
