I move in amendment:-
That the said Bill he amended fey adding thereto the following sections: Sections 75 and 76 of the said Act are repealed and the following sections are substituted therefor.
This amendment will be found on page 1238 of the Votes and Proceedings. It is to provide that in the first place the writ for an election shall be dated and be returnable on such day as the Governor General determines, or the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery may determine in cases where such clerk has' authority to so determine, pursuant to the Act respecting the House of Commons. That would be required to be followed by an amendment I have already presented, providing that after certain delay, in case there should be a vacancy in the representation, the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery shall have authority to issue the writ himself so that no constituency shall remain unrepresented for a longer period than three months. The next section 76 provides- that the returning officer shall be one of a certain class. In Ontario the sheriff or registrar of deeds, in the province of Quebec the registrar or sheriff or pro-thonotary, in the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, the sheriff, in Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Yukon Territory, the sheriff or registrar or deputy registrar or the superintendent of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. There are further supplementary provisions for any case in .which a sufficient number of officers cannot be found or in case of their disqualification, or disability or refusal to act. The object of the section is, in fact, that persons of a particular class and qualification shall be selected, and in that way, it is

believed, some of the unfortunate occurrences which occasionally have taken place in this country will be prevented in the future, because this will assure the country that men of responsible position are selected for this important post.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
So far as I am able to observe from a brief examination of the amendment, the principal difference between our present law and the amendment seems to be as to the persons to whom the writ of election shall be directed. Our present law provides that the writ shall be directed to the person appointed by the Governor in Council as the returning officer. The proposition in the amendment is that certain named officials shall be appointed returning officers. I am not, at the moment, able to say how long our statute has been in its present condition, but it is certainly many years-I should say at least twenty-five or thirty years-and, during that time, the writs have been addressed at each election to such returning officer as was selected for the purpose by the Governor in Council. In Ontario, with which province I am more familiar than with any other, the opposite rule prevailed, and, for a great many years-probably for quite as long a time-the writs were required to be addressed to officials just as is proposed in this amendment. That system seems not to have been satisfactory; two years ago the legislature of Ontario, under the leadership of tlie present government, changed it and adopted our system. In these circumstances, the experience of the past and the trend of legislation would seem to be in favour of continuing the system which we have maintained so long in Dominion elections, and I would submit that no good reason for the change appears.
Amendment negatived.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
What is the veason for this amendment ?
Mr, HENDERSON. We consider it a good, loyal thing to do.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

I move that the Bill be amended by adding thereto the following section :
Section 77 of the said Act is further amended by adding thereto the following subsection:
2. Every person who, at a time when by this or any other Act' he is disqualified from acting as returning officer, deputy returning officer, election clerk or poll clerk, nevertheless so acts, is, disqualified from voting at any Dominion election during the period of seven years from the date of his first official act as such returning officer, deputy returning officer, election clerk or poll clerk, and he is also guilty of an indictable offence., and shall, on conviction, be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year nor less than six months, with or without hard labour.
By reference to the notice of motion at page 1239 of the Votes and Proceedings, it will be seen that I am changing the motion as there given by striking out the words ' without prosecution for or conviction of any offence.' It seems to me that this is a proposition which ought to commend itself to the judgment of the House.

I move the folowing amendment :
Section 114 of said Act is repealed and the following is substituted therefor :
Section 114 of the Act, I may say, reads as follows :
The returning officer shall, at least two days before the day fixed for polling, furnish to each candidate or his agent a list of all deputy returning officers appointed to act in such election with the name or number of the

polling station at which each of them is to act.
This must be done two days before the polling, and all he has to furnish is the names. Unless he gives the residence and occupation, the name is of little use. I propose that the following be substituted :
114. The returning officer shall, at least three clear days, next before the date fixed for polling, deliver to the official agent of each candidate, a last of all the deputy returning officers and poll clerks who will act in such election, stating the post office address and occupation or addition of each such officer, and the name or number of the polling station at which each of them is to act.
Then X propose to repeal section 116 of the said Act and substitute the following therefor :
116. Each deputy returning officer shall furnish to the returning officer, not later than nine o'clock in the morning of the fifth day prior to the day fixed for polling, the name, post office address and occupation, or addition of such poll clerk ; and the returning officer shall, not later than twelve o'clock noon of the day on which he receives such particulars, post up in his office a list of the deputy returning officers and poll clerks, with the post office address and occupation or addition of each, showing the polling station where each is to act, and shall permit free access to and afford full opportunity for inspection of such list by any candidate, agent or elector at all reasonable times, until the polls are closed. No person shall be appointed a deputy returning officer or poll clerk who is not a resident of and a voter in tbe municipality, parish, or other local territorial division wherein the polling subdivision in which he is to act is situate, or, in the case of unorganized territory, who is not a resident of, and a voter in the electoral district.
This latter provision as to residence is taken from the Ontario statutes and is certainly a very necessary one. Cases have arisen, and the Minister of Justice is well aware of them, where the absence of such a provision has worked great hardship and allowed frauds to be practised.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have not been able to follow fully the alterations that my hon. friend is proposing, but so far as I can understand them, the change is with regard to what the returning officer is to do in the way of delivering to the agents a list of the deputies from two days to three days before the election. Now, Is it worth amending a statute for the sake of changing two days to three days, and about a matter of this character? I think any one who has had any experience with elections knows that it is frequently difficult enough for a returning officer to get the whole list of his deputies complete even two days before voting day. I have known many an Instance in which the day before voting day it was uncertain who was going to act as deputy at a particular poll.
It is not always possible to make your arrangements perfect two days before the election, and where the returning officer has 40 or 50 polls to look after, and some perhaps more than that, many miles away from where he lives, you are putting a needless burden upon him to say that he must do these things three days before election day. Then section 116 of the Act as it stands is the one which provides what the returning officer must do as to the poll clerks. The deputies, under the Act as it now stands, are to furnish to the returning officer not later than 9 o'clock in the morning of the day before voting, the name and occupation of each poll clerk, but that is not applicable to the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Yukon. But my hon. friend Is proposing to make that applicable to the whole Dominion, to strike out the words ' if practicable ' and make It imperative upon these officials to do what, in all human probability, is going to be impossible over half the constituencies In the country.

Something might be done if my hon. friend does not wash to accept the amendment altogether. I do not think that in the whole Act there is one clause which is so much transgressed as this one. It is difficult to get the names of the deputy returning officers even one day before the election, and in some cases there is deliberate neglect. There might be added a penalty for a returning officer not doing it according to the old law, say three days or two days, but impose a penalty. I can give an example in the election in St. James, Montreal, where, to my knowledge, ten or fifteen deputies were changed during the night preceding the votation. I happened to be a candidate there and I asked the returning officer for the names of the deputies. They were changed three or four times, and the last time about 8 o'clock at night previous to the day of election. When I got the names the last time I said to the returning officer :	Now, surely these are
the men who are going to act to-morrow ? He promised they would, and still some of them were changed again on the morning of the day of votation. This, as I say, was done for a purpose, because it was shown afterwards that the election was stolen, and it was due in great part to the deputy returning officers. There should be a penalty attached to that clause by which a returning officer, if he does not give the names of his deputies two days or three days before the polling, should be punished. It seems to me that we are all interested in securing that the elections should be carried on as honestly as possible, and the best wTay to secure that end is to see that at least the officials appointed by the government shall do their duty. Now, evidently parliament is convinced that something of that sort should be done, because we

have a law saying so. But if the government does not want to go as far as the amendment of my hon. friend, at least they ought to add a penalty for neglect of duty bv the returning officer. I would suggest that the returning officer, within two days preceding polling, should give the names of all his deputies, and if he changes any one of them after having given the names to the candidates, he shall be condemned to pay a penalty.
I submit that no good purpose can be served by that amendment; in fact, what object is there in having the names of the deputy returning officers ? Why should any one want them?
My hon. friend is convinced that the law as it exists to-day is useless?

I would rather see the [provision taken away than enlarged. 1 want to tell my hon. friend that he cannot carry that law out in the riding I represent, nor even in any riding in New Ontario, because of the great distance.
It is carried out in provincial elections.

It is not carried out in provincial elections. I have known returning officers to be sent away three or four days before the day of polling and not be able to reach the polling place. The electors gathered there had to elect their own returning officer to conduct the polls. That has occurred frequently, and the law provides for it.

The returning officer has eight days in which to choose his deputies. Why should he not choose them before ? In a county where it is known there is to be an election the returning officer should be prepared the day after nomination to give the names of his deputies to the two candidates.
In a district like mine there might be great difficulties, a man might agree to act as deputy and then be prevented by absence or illness. Then the object of knowing the deputy might be a bad object.
The object would be to see that he is an honest man.
Many of the worst evils in the Ontario elections were due to the employment of outsiders to do work which no man in the constituency was base enough to do.

The minister did not refer to the last five lines of this amendment.
Mi-. AYLESWORTH. That is the requirement that no one shall lie appointed deputy or poll clerk unless he is a resident of and voter in the municipality, in the poll-Mr. BERGERON.
ing division. That would be very objectionable. Many of our best poll clerks and deputies are young law students, not 21 years of age, who are sent from county towns into the country and conduct their polls perhaps more satisfactorily than any one else.
Amendment negatived.

What does the Prime Minister say about the necessity of postponing these elections ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am told there are some provinces where it would be absolutely impracticable to hold them all on the same day. The member for Yale-Carl-boo said it would be impossible in his own riding.

I have information of an absolutely different character with regard to every riding in British Columbia. I made careful inquiries there last autumn and I find that all the provincial elections are held on the same day without difficulty. Mr. Smitli-Curtis, a Liberal candidate, is thus reported :
Mr. Smith-Curtis particularly emphasized his desire for a clean campaign and emphatically declared that he did not favour a deferred election in the Kootenay Riding, believing it to be in the true interests of every elector that the voting in Kootenay should take place on the day of the general elections throughout Canada.
That is strong testimony from a Liberal candidate in one of the postponed ridings and I have not heard anything in this House or elsewhere to induce me to believe that the Kootenay is in a different position from the other deferred ridings in British Columbia.

My hon. friend's information was certainly very bad. In my first election in Burrard, the returning officer was not able even in a by-election to get the ballot boxes into the northern part of the riding, which is now Comox-Atlin until four days after the date set for holding the elections. How could the ballot boxes leave say Nanaimo and get into Telegraph Creek and Atlin, which is 14 days in the winter, and at the same time get into the Squamish Yalley ? It is a phy-

sical impossibility to have the Comox-Atlin election at the same time as the others and the same thing applies to Yale-Cariboo.

The local elections are held on the same day and why could it not be done in federal elections ?
Mr. MAiCPHERSON. The local constituencies are smaller. If a polling booth is not represented you may upset the election.
I do not understand when the provincial elections can all be held on the one day why the Dominion can not.

It is impossible to reach the remote parts of that constituency in a week with the ballot boxes. I assure the leader of the opposition, who wants to be fair, that the information is not correct that you could reach any point in Comox-Atlin and get your ballots printed and distributed within the time stated.

I have no doubt of the sincerity of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Macpherson) but I am a little inclined to discount statements of that kind because I was assured two years ago of the absolute impossibility of bringing about the election in Kootenay on the same day as the others, and now I find the Liberal candidate in Kootenay saying there is no difficulty whatever. In every local constituency in British Columbia the election takes place on the the same day, and it is a perfectly simple thing for the sheriff by employing a sufficient force of men to send the ballot boxes throughout the three or four local constituencies comprised in one Dominion riding.	-
That is different.

There is not the slightest difficulty about doing the same thing in a Dominion election provided you employ enough men to do it. I have a telegram from the premier of British Columbia stating that not the slightest difficulty was experienced in the last provincial election. If the returning officer employs four men to do the work which four returning officers did in the four provincial constituencies, it follows logically that what was done in the provincial elections can be done iu the Dominion elections. I would say to the Prime Minister that I have a telegram dated the 4th of this month from the Prime Minister of British Columbia in which after referring to a report in the local press of a statement in this House that the elections in Yale-Cariboo could not be held simultaneously with those in the rest of the province he says : I
I desire to give the strongest denial to this. Provincial elections held simultaneously gave every satisfaction and proved there is no difficulty in carrying this out.
He goes on to say that there is no reason whatever why the election in Yale-Cariboo should be held at a later date than the elections.in the rest of the province.

You have got to have your ballots printed at a given point and the ballots have to be sent to a different polling subdivision. There are 1,500 miles between the southern and northern districts of Comox-Atlin and if the ballots are printed in Nanaimo how can you get into Surprise lake without a flying machine in the time allowed. The best possible time that can be made to Surprise lake is 11 days, and if there is ice upon the river as there was during my own election when the man who carried the ballot boxes was obliged to break the trail for 80 miles with dogs, how can you overcome a difficulty like that. When the Prime Minister of British Columbia states it is possible to do that, he states what any man who knows the country knows to be incorrect.

I suppose he knows it is correct because it has been done and done in the winter during the last provincial elections. Let me point out that the difficulty is not with regard to the ballots but in posting the proclamations announcing the elections. You have seven days additional to distribute the ballots. I repeat that by employing four men to do the work which the four returning officers would do in .the nrovincial elections you can undoubtedly accomplish in a Dominion election what was accomplished in the dead of winter during the last provincial election.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. gentleman who represents the district (Mr. Duncan Ross) has stated that he saw no personal advantage in having the election held after the other elections because as he said the organization has all gone to pieces the moment the result of the general election is known. We have the testimony of Mr. McBride on the one side ana the testimony of the hon. member (Mr. Duncan Ross) on the other, and I think we might as well let it go as proposed.
Let me point out that in the county of Gaspe we formerly had the nomination a fortnight before the election.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Once.

Yet it worked well. The nomination was held a fortnight before the election and the election was held on the same day as the other elections thus carrying out the principle which the Prime Minister has so often advocated, that all elections should be held on the same day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This exception applies to only 5 constituencies out of 221.
And the less we have of these exceptions the better.
The argument which my hou. friend (Mr. Macpherson) has used with regard to Comox-Atlin does not apply to Yale-Cariboo because no such difficulties exist in that constituency.

Does the Prime Minister press this provision with reference to the election in Kootenay, notwithstanding the declaration of his own candidate that there is no necessity for it ?
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, I do not know the particulars about it.
Amendment negatived.

I propose to move an amendment which has to some extent the same object as the one that has just been discussed. It is an alternative amendment numbered 17 in the Votes and Proceedings, and is found on pages 1239, 1240 and 1241. The' object of this amendment is to secure the holding of all the elections in Canada on the same day except in the Yukon Territory. It will apply to the five or six electoral districts in which the elections are now usually postponed. The object is accomplished by advancing the preliminary stages of the election, the proceedings as to those which require a greater amount of time for preparation being taken at an earlier stage. For instance, writs of election shall be despatched to the returning officers in the case of those electoral districts in time to allow the lapse of twenty-one clear days between the day of their receipt by the returning officer and the day fixed for the nomination of the candidates. The nomination day will be fourteen days instead of seven days before the election. The general provision found on page 1240 as subsection 2 is that in the case or cases of any electoral district or districts in which the Governor in Council may, after due inquiry conclude that the proclamation aforesaid cannot otherwise be posted up so as to allow the required time between such posting up and the nomination day, the" Governor in Council shall fix the day of nomination in the way that I have referred to ; so that it is left to the Governor in Council to determine in any special ease whether these special provisions shall apply, and in such cases he shall have them to apply in such a way that we shall secure all the elections in Canada on the same day.

Surely the Prime Minister wdll accept this amendment. Has he lost confidence in the schemes that have been concocted, that he requires the elections in those districts to be held after the general election ? Is it because he knows that if the elections were held in those districts on the day of the general election, each of them would return an opponent of the government ? I think we are voting some $238,000,000, excluding the lead bounties ; and surely with that amount of Mr. BERGERON.
money the government party ought to have confidence that they can win the country, particularly in these hard times, when they have lost the old cry of 1 Luck and Laurier,' and.ought to be willing to have all the elections held on the same day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am satisfied, I am sure, but there are some doubting Thomases in this House. I heard this afternoon that some hon. gentlemen were only waiting for the elections to put us out. Therefore they will have all the advantages.

Many other people must share the feelings of these doubting Thomases.
Amendment negatived.

I propose :
(18) That the said Bill he amended by adding thereto the following section :-
Section 129 of the said Act is repealed and the following is substituted therefor :-
" 129. The printer, and in case of an incorporated company, one of the executive officers of the said company, shall, upon delivery of the ballot papers to the returning officer, file in his hands an affidavit of such printer or executive officer, sworn before such returning officer, setting forth the description of the ballot papers so printed, the number of ballot papers supplied to such returning officer, and stating the facts that no other ballot paper or ballot papers was or were printed or have been supplied to any one else or remain in his possession or under his control."
Tile object of the amendment is manifest with the reading of it, and I will not trouble the House witli any enlargement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not able to see what improvement there is in the amendment as compared with the existing law. In the present law the printer is required to make the affidavit. The proposition is that the printer, or, if it is an incorporated company, one of the executive officers of the company, shall make the affidavit. I think it would be much better that the printer should make the affidavit than some officer of a company who probably knows nothing about it, except what the printer tells him. Under the present law the printer who makes the affidavit is certainly some man who might be prosecuted for perjury. If the printing is done in the printing office of an incorporated company, the present law would require somebody who answered the description of the printer of these ballot papers' to make the affidavit accounting for them. The other provision of this amendment is to require the affidavit to be made before the returning officer. I do not know why one officer should be preferred to another for swearing the affidavit before. I do not know the purpose of the amendment unless it is simply for the purpose of making amendments.

The Minister of Justice must know that many of these ballot papers are very badly printed, and in some cases there are not enough ballots. They are printed, 1 understand, in various offices, the paper is sometimes poor, and sometimes the ballots are spoiled before they are used. Surely we cannot take too many precautions to see that we have proper ballot papers.
Amendment negatived
In accordance with the amendment of the hon. member for West Hastings I propose clause No. 19. As the motion of the hon. member was accepted, this follows as a consequence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not suppose any one can have any objection except that it is difficult to understand how this is necessary. Under the present law the deputy returning officer is required, in the presence of the candidates, their agents, and such electors as are present to open the ballot box and ascertain that there are no ballot papers or other papers therein. It is not made any stronger by requiring him to see that the ballot box is absolutely empty. Piling up adjectives and adverbs does not make the thing stronger.
There may be in the ballot box, as there were in the ballot boxes at Addington, secret compartments or mechanism by which the ballot papers may be secretly stored in the box.

This will call the attention of the deputy returning officer to the fact that such appliances might be there. He may never have heard of such cases having arisen, and it may be well to call his attention to the fact that appliances of that sort have been devised by scoundrels to defeat the will of the people.
Amendment negatived.

I beg to move amendment No. 21 which will be found on page 1241 of the Votes and Proceedings. It requires the printer's affidavit to form part of the return made by the deputy returning officer to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery.
Amendment negatived.

I move the following amendment to be found on page 1241 of the Votes and Poceedings:
(22) That the said Bill he amended by adding thereto the following section :-
Section 226 of the said Act is repealed and the following is substituted therefor
" 226. No person who has voted at an election shall, in any legal proceeding questioning the election or return, or before any parliamentary committee or any commission, be required to state for whom he voted, but he may so state, and if he do so, his statement shall be received in evidence."
The present law states that no one who has voted at an election shall be required
to say for whom he voted, and I understand that even in cases where the voter was willing to make such a statement, it has been held by the court that counsel had not the right to put the question to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This would certainly destroy the secrecy of the ballot because if you have a poll of say 100 votes and there have been 48 ballots cast one way and 52 the other, and you allow each one of the 52 men to state for whom he has voted, that would disclose at once how the other 48 voted; and while the 52 men may be quite willing to make the declaration the other 48 may not, and they may be just those around whom the law throws the protection of secrecy. Would it be advisable to change that ? The present law extends to no collateral proceeding. It does not extend to any prosecution for a criminal offence where it may be important to determine how the ballot was marked but only to a proceeding to unseat the successful candidate. In any proceeding questioning the election the voter is protected by its being illegal to ask him in court how he voted. I think it would be a very serious step to change that and make that inroad upon the feature of this Ballot Act, to which every one, apparently, attaches the utmost importance, unless you are prepared to do away with the element of secrecy altogether and say that the voter, if he pleases to do so, may mark his ballot openly on the table before everybody or identify himself by some writing on the paper.

So far as secrecy is concerned, if it is once conceded that you can obtain the information in some collateral proceeding you leave the door as open as in the case proposed. It makes no difference whether the information is acquired in a proceeding questioning the election and return or in some collateral proceeding, tlie secrecy of the ballot in the case mentioned by the minister will be departed from to that extent. The question came before the committee that investigated or tried to investighte-or some members of which tried to investigate-the West Huron and Brockville election frauds, and, after a great deal of discussion, it was decided that the witnesses might be asked for whom they voted. The object of this amendment is to make it clear that the witness cannot be compelled to state for whom he voted, but may do so if he is willing. It seems to me that this is better than the law at present.
Amendment negatived.

I move that the Bill be amended by adding a section immediately after section 258. This section, No. 258, is the section dealing with secrecy of the poll and containing provisions as to cases which are declared to be illegal in that con-

neetion. The effect of this amendment is to increase the penalty upon the election officer who is guilty of any infraction of the provisions of this section.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What is the present penalty?

A line not exceeding $200 and imprisonment for not more than six months. This provides for a fine of not less than $100 or more than $200, imprisonment for not less than six months and not more than twelve and disfranchisement.
* Mr. LALOR. I wish to call the attention of the committee to the way the secrecy of the ballot poll is sometimes carried out in the county I represent-and I do not think the penalty can be too severe on the election officers in the poll for failure to carry out the secrecy of the polling booth in their charge. In the county of Haldimand- and I do not say that the Liberal party is altogether responsible for this state of things, for I fear the practice might have been tried to some extent before the Liberal party got possession of the polling booths -a system of telegraphing is carried out, and has been for years, by which a sign is thrown from the deputy returning officer to the constable and from him to somebody else, and in that way it is known how the elector votes ; and, if there is any money going, he is paid. I hope the government will make the penalty for violating the secrecy of the polls as great as it ought to be, for we want secrecy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This practice that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lalor) speaks of is an illegal practice. Have there been anv prosecutions for the violation of the Act?
I do not think so. But, notwithstanding, I state the facts on my responsibility.
Is there any description anywhere in the law of what should be the divisions of the polling booths?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Oh, yes.

Then it is not carried out. Generally a polling booth is one room. A curtain is hung in one corner. Of course, if anybody wants to go behind the curtain and make his cross his ballot is secret, because those in the booth cannot see through the curtain, nor can they see over it, for it is generally six feet or more high. But if the voter must have his cross made by the deputy returning officer and gees behind the curtain accompanied by the deputy and the two agents, when he states for whom he wishes to vote everybody in the booth can hear him, so that there is clearly no secrecy about such a ballot. I understand the law to mean that there shall be an entirely different room, so that when it is.
necessary to ask a voter for whom he votes his answer may be heard by the deputy returning officer, but not by others in the polling booth.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The only objection I can suggest to this amendment is that it is making anomalies and discrepancies in the different penalties even greater than they are. It is in the direction of greater severity, and I am content.
Amendment agreed to.

I desire now to move an amendment to which I will ask the particular attention of the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). I propose to insert the following as section 278a :
278a. Every person who, directly or indirectly, by himself or by any person on his behalf before or during an election, in order to induce, or in such manner as might induce any voter or class of voters in a particular electoral district to vote for or against any candidate, or to refrain from voting by publio speaking, by any writing, by any printed publication, or otherwise, offers or promises, or offers or promises to procure or endeavour to procure, or suggests the probability of the expenditure of the public moneys of Canada, within the electoral district or districts, if and in case only such voter or voters procure or assist to procure the return of a particular candidate or of a candidate of a particular political party, or who, with the intent or in manner aforesaid, threatens or promises to impede, delay, hinder, prevent or diminish such expenditure, is guilty of the indictable offence of bribery, and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year and not less than six months, and shall forfeit the sum of one thousand dollars to any person who sues therefor, with costs.
This is a new provision not found in the present law. I am not wedded to the exact phraseology, and if the government approve the principle and desire to make any modifications I am willing. But the principle is one that no government can afford to ignore.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I must confess that my hon. friend, in advocating this amendment, is rising to a height that I am entirely unable to reach. I cannot look upon what he depicts in this amendment as in the nature of a corrupt practice. To my mind it is not more than any public man with propriety may do in discussing a matter of public interest in the electoral district in which he may happen to be addressing the electors. Every candidate in offering himself for the suffrages of any locality or district, is identifying himself with that locality, is undertaking either tacitly or expressly, that he will exert himself to the utmost in the interest of the electors of the locality which sends him to parliament. If he, as a member of parliament, by advocating the expenditure of public money upon some public work in that locality, is able to benefit

his constituency, I am unable to see any impropriety in his doing so, in parliament or anywhere else. He is not doing that for the benefit of one political party more than another, he is advocating the cause of the electors generally of the constituency that sends him to parliament and it seems to me he is doing a legitimate thing. I regard that as a public question upon which any one who offers himself as a candidate for a public position is expected to have views, and ought to express those views with freedom and with candour. I wish to say and I wish to say it without any intention of giving offence, that I can see no difference in principle between advocating a public building, a public wharf, or any other public work in a constituency, and advocating the giving of better terms in any manner you please to any province of the Dominion, either in giving to a province an increased subsidy, or in giving to a province better terms as to control over its public lands or any other public property. If the one is a corrupt practice, it seems to me the other is. But I think that neither of them is corrupt, and that such candidate is simply advocating in a proper manner that which he believes is in the public interest, either of a whole province, or of a smaller section, or community, township, or any other local subdivision.

The Minister of Justice entirely loses sight of the purview of the amendment. The question is not whether a public man has a right to advocate the erection of a public building, or the expenditure of public money in a particular locality, but the question is whether he has the right to do so with the view of influencing votes in that electoral district. If it is represented that this work will be erected if a certain man is returned, and that it will not be erected if he is not returned, that is what the section is aimed at.

The section is not designed to touch discussion in parliament at all, it is not designed to prevent a eondi-date from declaring a particular policy in regard to any subject such as the Minister of Justice has suggested, but it Is designed to prevent wholesale bribery of a community by saying that if this particular candidate is elected then a certain expenditure will be made and If this particular candidate is not elected that particular .expenditure will not be made. It seems to me there is no difference between inducements of that kind held1 out to a whole class or an entire community, and the individual corruption of bribery of electors one by one.

I think my hon. friend from Prince Edward (Mr. Alcorn) must be very sanguine if after looking over the list of supplementary estimates and the long list, the treble column list, of subsidies to railways and things of that sort he expects the 414
Prime Minister to accept this amendment. If he remembers some of the promises that were held out by a certain candidate in the election of 1904, he must have a good deal of faith if he thinks the Minister of Justice would be inclined to accept that, or if he remembers the time the citizens of a certain section were to get the present of a magnificent clock if they voted for a certain candidate, and when it was held out to them that if a certain candidate were elected a canal would run in a certain direction, whereas if he were not elected, the canal would not run in that direction. All these promises have been held out by candidates upon the government side, and my hon. friend must have been very hopeful to expect that the Prime Minister and his colleagues would accept the amendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is something in that. Demands for public works of every description are growing upon the government. I have had so many demands from hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House during the present session that it has been a great sorrow to us not to have been able to gratify them all. I think the hon. gentlemen from Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler) himself was pressing upon us a demand for certain works and it was quite proper.
More than that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is enough then.

Surely the Prime Minister must admit that a member of parliament may interest himself in getting certain public works for his constituency. Why, even the Minister of Public Works reproached me on altogether false premises for not having asked for what I had repeatedly asked. The Minister of Public Works was not in the House at the time, he was devoting himself to another sphere of politics where he was very active. However, a member of parliament certainly has a right to ask for these things for his constituency, he has a right to try and influence the government to put public works of a necessary character in his constituency. But surely the Prime Minister sees a difference between that and a candidate going into a constituency and saying, if you elect me the canal shall come out at Port Hope, and if you do not elect me, it is going to come out at Trenton. Would the Prime Minister say that was a proper thing ? Is not that holding out a bribe to the constituency to vote in a certain way ? And where So you distinguish between that and the offer to a poor voter of a $5 bill? The only difference is that you are doing it by wholesale In the one case, and you are doing it by retail in the other, and that is precisely what the amendment of my hon. friend from Prince Edward desires to prevent.
Amendment negatived.

I would have been glad to see in the law a provision preventing a candidate from presenting himself in more than one county. But I understand that cannot be done, especially since a man may be put into nomination without his consent. I have an amendment in the Votes and Proceedings to the effect that when a man has been elected in one or more counties he should be compelled to send in his resignation of the county or counties for which he does not elect to sit within thirty days after he has been so elected, that resignation to be sent to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, as there would be no Speaker at the time. In case he does not do this within thirty days, the seat can be declared vacant, but the fact of electing to choose one county will not prevent the member from having that election tested before the courts. If one election is contested no writ will be issued until the petition is disposed of.	.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not aware that there have been very many abuses of this kind. I remember Sir John Macdonald was elected in 1882 for Carle-ton and another constituency, but I think a couple of years elapsed before he was elected, because one of the elections was controverted.
The Postmaster General did the same thing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Suppose his election is controverted, would you force him to elect while the petition was before the courts?

There are the cases of Sir John Macdonald and Mr. Prefontaine who sat a couple of sessions before electing for which county he would sit. The object of this is to prevent a county from being unrepresented in this House for two sessions.
Suppose a member is disqualified on a petition from one county, what would my hon. friend do ?

If my hon. friend was elected for Gaspe and Nicolet and according to this amendment would have sent in his letters to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, saying he has made choice of the county of Gaspe, it would not prevent any one protesting his election in Nicolet. If he was disqualified for any act done in Nicolet, he would be deprived of two seats, because no man who is disqualified can sit in parliament.
My hon. friend is arguing against an old maxim in England that a man can stand for one, two. three or four counties.
That does not prevent that.

It does not prevent him standing, it only prevents him sitting.
Amendment, Mr. Bergeron, negatived.

I beg to move amendment No. 26 at page 1243 of tbe Votes and Proceedings. That amendment reads:
Subsection one of sectioto 269 of the said Act is amended by striking out all the words from and including the word ' shall ' in the 15th line, and by adding the following words in lieu thereof : ' is guilty of a corrupt practice, and liable to a penalty of $200 to any person who sues thereof with costs, and shail also upon conviction be imprisoned for one year.
This is an amendment to the intimidation section and it makes intimidation a corrupt practice. The law provides for the forfeiture of $200 and there is added to this that he shall also be imprisoned for one year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I cannot see the reason for this amendment. It provides that undue influence shall be a corrupt practice, but that is expressly made so now by section 278 and is frequently a corrupt practice which avoids an election. The amendment reduces the present penalty, as it is now an indictable offence which makes the offender liable to five years' imprisonment besides the penalty' of $200.
Amendment negatived.
Bill reported.

maintopic: USE OF TOBACCO BY YOUNG PERSONS.

speechtext: Consideration of amendments made by the Senate to Bill (No. 173) to restrain the use of tobacco by young persons.-Mr. Aylesworth.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: USE OF TOBACCO BY YOUNG PERSONS.
speechtext:
The most impox-tant amendment made by the Senate is the reduction of the age from 18 to 16 years. The Bill as introduced in this House fixed the age at 16 but by amendment in committee it was made 18 years. The Senate has also amended the provision of the Act with regard to the confiscation of tobacco which may be in possession of a young person of 16 years so as to include the chewing as well as the smoking of tobacco and to authorize the constable to confiscate any tobacco which he finds in possession of a young person under 16, either smoking, chewing, or about to smoke or chew. There is an addition of a subsection to the third section which imposes a penalty on juveniles smoking in any street or public place. To that is added :
It shall be the duty of the justice to examine upon oath or affirmation all persons brought before him who are found guilty of a violation of this section, as to where or from whom such persons purchased or obtained the cigarettes or cigarette paper or

tobacco found in the possession of any such person, and the refusal to Rive such information to the satisfaction of the justice shall be deemed a contempt of the court.
Some bon. MEMBERS. Question.
Motion (Mr. Aylesworth) concurred in ; amendments read a second time and agreed
I think this latter provision does not add anything to the general law. If any person under oath is asked such a question he would have no privilege to refuse to answer and he would he guilty of contempt of court if he did not answer. I beg to move the adoption of the amendments.

maintopic: USE OF TOBACCO BY YOUNG PERSONS.
speechtext:
I move :
That the amendments of the Senate be not received and that the Bill be referred back to the committee of the House for further consideration.

maintopic: USE OF TOBACCO BY YOUNG PERSONS.
speechtext: This amendment of the Senate refers to juveniles smoking or chewing or ' about to smoke or chew tobacco.' How is it possible to say whether any one is ' about to smoke or chew tobacco.' I do not think absurdity could possibly go further than our friends of the Senate have gone.

maintopic: USE OF TOBACCO BY YOUNG PERSONS.
speechtext: I particularly object to the Senate amendment by which the age limit is changed from 18 years to 16. Hon. Senator Power introduced that amendment and his strongest argument was based on the statement that 16 years was the limit in the provinces. I beg to point out that 18 years is the age limit in Ontario and New Brunswick. The Hon. Senator referred to the use of tobacco as being a minor offence. I do not think it is the desire of this House to punish youths for smoking tobacco because it is a moral wrong, but rather because the use of tobacco by persons of that age produces ill effects physically. Senator David in support of the 16 year age limit stated that boys of 16 years are very often earning their own living-

maintopic: USE OF TOBACCO BY YOUNG PERSONS.
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: USE OF TOBACCO BY YOUNG PERSONS.

maintopic: USE OF TOBACCO BY YOUNG PERSONS.

The motion of the Minister of Justice is that the amendments be concurred in. If that motion is negatived it would have the same result as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Miller) seeks to attain.
to.

Bill (No. 204) to amend chapter 38 of the statutes of 1907 in amendment of the Railway Act-Mr. Aylesworth-read a second time, and the House went into committee thereon.
Mr. AlrLESWORTH. An Act of last session, chapter 38, provided for the deposit with the Secretary of State of mortgages on railway property to secure debentures. The statute provides the effect of such deposit to be in substance the same as the effect of filing a chattel mortgage in the office of sonie official of the county in which the property is situated. It makes it valid as against the claims of subsequent creditors, mortgages or purchasers. The next clause in like manner provided that a mortgage on rolling stock given by the railway company and filed with the Secretary of State should be a valid security against the claims of subsequent creditors. Then comes the provision which it is desired to repeal. That is a provision that in the case of any company possessing rolling stock and mortgaging it for the purpose of securing such debentures, the like deposit shall have the same effect as in the case of a railway company. That provision seems to me to be of very questionable validity. It is doubtful, at all events, whether this parliament has any jurisdiction under the British North America Act to pass any such provision relating not to the undertaking or property of a railway company, but simply to property within the province. The other clauses of the Act are in connection with legislation upon a subject which is within our jurisdiction, that of railway law generally, and are certainly valid with reference to Dominion railway companies. This clause is, however, of at least questionable character, and as soon as it was observed, attention was called to it by the Deputy Minister of Justice writing a letter within a day or two after prorogation to the legal gentleman at whose instance these clauses were inserted in the Bill. They were inserted in the Senate, and the retention of this particular clause was through some misunderstanding between that legal gentleman and the deputy minister, who was conferred with on the subject before the amendment was introduced. It would possibly be a snare to companies possessed of rolling stock, who might rely on this provision if it remained on the statute-book, and it was thought that it should at the earliest opportunity be repealed. On section 2,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This section stood for revision, with a view to including in the benefits of the section not only the volunteers who had enlisted in the Canadian corps for service in South Africa, but also Canadians or persons resident in Canada who have served in South Africa in any British corps, and also for the purpose of including nurses who were attached to military forces. The amendment as drafted to cover these points reads as follows :
This Act shall apply to all volunteers then Qomieiled in Canada who served with the British forces in South Africa during the years 1899 to 1902, or who, being so domiciled, enlisted with or were appointed to Canadian corps that arrived in South Africa for the purpose of so serving, but owing to the close of the war were not on active service.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There were teachers ; but it is not my intention to include any but those who are mentioned in this section.

As I had1 the honour of first bringing to the attention of the House the suggestion that all volunteers who went to South Africa, whether coming from the prairie provinces or other parts of Canada, should be entitled to this grant, I am pleased to know that the government has at last decided to give effect to this policy by introducing the present motion.

I approve of this very much, and I am only sorry that my hon. friend has not found himself in a position, with all the lands we have in the Northwest, to offer something to the men who fought on the frontier in 18G6 and 1870. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This proposes to strike out the words ' sixty-seven ' in the Act and substitute 1 sixty-nine '' in order to provide for the additional district judges.

The other day I asked the right lion, the First Minister if he intended acting upon the recommendation of the Quebec local legislature, which declared that two more judges were needed in the district of Montreal and one in the district of Quebec. He replied that the government had decided to confer with the different provinces before granting their de-

mands. He thought there were sufficient judges iu Quebec and the other provinces it the systems in these provinces were changed. I find it strange now that he should call on us to appoint judges in the other provinces and not in the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I read in the ' Hansard ' the other day the answer made by the leader of the House to the hon. gentleman's question. I have really nothing to add to what the First Minister then said.
I am aware that the Quebec legislature has passed the necessary legislation providing for additional j-dges and that these additonal appointments have been the subject of correspondence between the Department of Justice and the Department of the Attorney General of Quebec. The matter is one of considerable importance and practical difficulty. Under the British North America Act we have no voice in the passing of legislation which calls for additional judges in any province.
On the other hand, responsibility is upon the Dominion for the payment of judges and the providing of pensions. In these circumstances, while it may be that under the letter of the constitution, it was not contemplated that the province should in any way consult the Dominion qn the subject before passing its legislation calling for additional judges, it certainly would seem something that would conduce to harmony in the administration of the respective functions of the different governments if there could be an understanding beforehand, and if there could be some general arrangement by which it could be understood in practice that, before legislation of the sort I have described were passed, there would be at least a discussion of the necessity for it with the Dominion authorities. And I may say that steps in that direction have been taken, and an effort will be made to devise some means whereby there will be no danger of either the local legislatures taking action which might not afterwards be carried into effect as promptly as the local legislatures think it should be, or of taking action to provide for the appointment of additional judges where the necessity for them is not very apparent. [DOT] Now, in the case of the province of Quebec, unon all the information I have been able to obtain, there seems no actual lack, numerically speaking, at any rate, of judicial strength. The number of judges of the superior court already appointed throughout the province is considered to be ample to discharge the judicial work of the courts of the province if these were distributed in some different way. Business, as it stands, is congested in the cities of Quebec and Montreal, while in the rural districts there are, I am given to understand. more than one instance of judges who would be the better perhaps with a
little more to do ; and, at all events, where there is not such an amount of work that the judges as they are to-day are not able readily to overtake it and still have time on their hands. In these circumstances, if it were possible to work out some scheme by which there could be a somewhat more even distribution of the work by which the judges from the rural districts might be assigned a share in the heavier work of the cities, there would not seem to be the necessity for adding so considerably to the expense of our present judicial system as would be the case if a number of additional judges were appointed. The same condition of things exists in the province of Alberta, where the staff of judges was provided only a year ago; the provincial authorities are asking for additional judicial help in the superior court. This is a continually recurring difficulty, and, in view of the situation I have attempted to outline, it was thought that, for the present year at all events, we could not properly propose to the House to provide for additional judges where there were existing courts and a certain number of judges in those courts to do the work. As a result, this measure is restricted to providing salaries for two judges lor the new courts which have recently been established in New, or Northern Ontario, where settlers have gone in a long distance from any other court, and where an absolutely new court has in the ease of two districts been established ready to go to work on sending a judge for that purpose. In the same way, the new court in the northern part of the province of Manitoba, where an increase of settlement has caused an increase of judicial work, is called for by the legislature, and we have proposed, under this Bill, to provide a salary for that county court judge. But where there are existing courts and a certain number of existing judges, we have thought that the province ought to get along for another year at all events by making some change or otherwise, without asking the expense to be put upon the Dominion, which providing for additional judges would involve. ,
On section 2-Manitoba-judges of county courts.
This section simply increases the county court judges in Manitoba by two, I understand?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: By one. There was an increase of one last year, making the number seven ; it is now made eight.
When will the additional judge be appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I can only say that as soon as the Act is passed providing the salary the matter will be taken into

consideration. It has not yet been considered.

Then the hon. minister [DOT]cannot tell us who the proposed judge is?
On section 3-pension or chief or assistant chief of Board of Kailway Commissioners if previously a judge.

I understand that this amendment is to include the assistant chief commissioner,-though perhaps that has been'enacted already-and to reduce the period by which the pension shall be earned from fifteen years to twelve years ? What is the reason for that ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When the office of chief commissioner became vacant by the death of Mr. Killam, and it was a question of finding a successor, the position was offered to the present incumbent, Mr. Mabee. He at once pointed out that he would, by assuming the office, forfeit any right that was accruing to him to the enjoyment of a judicial pension. The Railway Act provides no pension. And that was a consideration which weighed very much in his mind. The statute provides for fifteen years' service as railway commissioner or five years of service as a judge and ten years' service as railway commissioner. This would not cover the ease of Mr. Mabee, as he had not been five years upon the bench. But he thought that some provision ought to be made in order that he would not, if he accepted the new work, forfeit the right which was accruing to him. It was thought that that was a reasonable request upon his part, and this change Is made entirely in that view. Mr. Mabee had been something over two years upon the bench, and would be covered by this provision if the amendment is made.
I do not see anything in section 21 about a period of five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The change is made substituting 12 for 15, or 2 for 5. The enactment was made in the first place on the occasion of Mr. Justice Killam leaving the Supreme Court and taking this position. In his case it made no difference, as he had seeu service on the bench for more than five years. I do not know why a period of 15 years or 5 years service on the bench was fixed.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

McCarthy. How idle it is to say this Bill should not pass. Two of its proposals have been before the House for flve or six years, the section relating to masters and mates and to marine engineers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The section of /the revised statutes which it is proposed to repeal provides that the Governor in Council may deal with the ships of any foreign country which gives us reciprocal coasting trade, but it does not apparently give us any power to discriminate either as to the different waters of Canada or as to the sizes of the vessels. The history of this measure is that some months ago we passed an order in council designed to repeal other orders which granted the privilege of our coasting trade to certain foreign countries. The United States do not give us reciprocal privileges and it does not apply to them. There are a number of foreign countries which grant us the privilege but it is practically of no value to us because we do not use their coasting trade. An order in council was passed declaring that after the 1st of January next these privileges granted by orders in council should be withdrawn. The order applies largely to Norwegian vessels, although its terms are broader than that. It has been represented to us that the Norwegians have adapted themselves particularly to the coal trade of the St. Lawrence, that many of the vessels in that trade are under the Norwegian flag, that some although built in the United Kingdom sail under the Norwegian flag, and of course, are only entitled to such privileges as Norwegian vessels may have. Many of the ships in the coal trade have been built specially for that trade and it has been represented that before the time fixed in the order in council the coal companies would be unable to obtain British ships of a proper class in sufficient numbers to handle the trade, and that if we adhere rigorously to the order in council we will practically prevent the coal companies getting tonnage to carry their coal. Of course nobody wante to do that. We have thought therefore that it is a case in which there should be some elasticity. We do not desire to extend the privileges of the coasting trade to these vessels without any limit, but it has been suggested that it might be expedient that the government should allow them to have the coasting trade for a limited time, and perhaps with regard to a limited class of tonnage, for instance, the smaller class of vessels would come into competition with our Canadian vessels while the larger vessels would not. It has been suggested that we might allow these larger Norwegian vessels to continue in the coasting trade for a limited period, and what that period should be is a fair matter for consideration. What we propose in this amendment is that instead of the existing clause in the revised statutes we should introduce a substitute clause which would give the government the power of discrimination. For example we might give the privilege to a Norwegian vessel in Atlantic waters and refuse her the privilege in the lake trade, or we might give her the privilege in the lake trade and refuse it on the Pacific coast or, we might agree

that Norwegian vessels up to say 1,000 or
2,000	tons should be excluded, but that vessels above that tonnage might be permitted temporarily to engage In the coal trade for a sufficient time to permit the coal companies to secure either Canadian or	British bottoms.	In other
words the purpose of this amendment is to allow elasticity in the law, whereby the government might adapt themselves to the special conditions which might be brought before them. But while we desire that, we wish to say it is not the intention of the government to recede from the general principle which has been laid down that these coasting privileges shall only be continued for a special purpose and for a limited time and under such circumstances as I have briefly mentioned to the House.

This is a very important measure which deeply concerns the shipping interests of the maritime provinces. We have continual protests from Canadian shipping interests against the encroachment of foreigners and the minister knows that this has been a great detriment to the shipping interests of the maritime provinces. The action taken by the order in council prohibiting Norwegians from coming into our territory was possibly a temporary step in the right direction, but it did not get down to the root of the evil. What Canada wants is some national idea to encourage the building of ships in the Dominion. Years ago when we had wooden ships built in the maritime provinces, we were one of the first maritime nations in the world and we had sufficient vessels to carry on our coasting trade. But now the Norwegians have come in, our shipping has become decadent and we are in this deplorable condition that the coal interests which this Bill is designed largely to benefit must have foreign tonnage.
The only way we can deal legitimately and nationally with that is to encourage shipbuilding in this country, and that is a question the government should take up instead of dilly dallying with measures of this kind. This question goes further. We have some remnants of the coasting trade left around the coasts of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island ; and under the system in vogue for a number of years past that coasting trade has been so oppressed by these large corporate interests, who have paid no attention to the local needs of the people, that it is not able to subsist, and will go out of business unless this government remedies the evils that assail it. These large foreign vessels come over under the coasting privilege, and as the minister lias told us, there is no relative value between the privileges we give to them and those accorded to us in the countries from which they come. Under the large incorporate interests which employ them, they shut out altogether the possibility of the small coasting tonnage of the maritime provinces get-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: ting its legitimate trade. Take the coal trade of Sydney, Inverness and Pictou. The hon. minister is surely aware of the disadvantages that smaller craft are suffering on account of the privileges given foreign tonnage and the abuse of those privileges, the large corporate companies supplying the coal of the maritime provinces to this foreign tonnage and to the prejudice of both the smaller coasting vessels and the people that they accommodate. Those evils are going on to-day just the same as last year and the year before.

Would the hon. gentleman permit me to say that two weeks ago, while at home, I made inquiries into that subject, so far as Pictou was concerned and I learned that every schooner that came there from Prince Edward Island or anywhere else had been loaded without the slightest delay, and the only trouble with our coal miners is that the schooners do not come as often as they like. The same thing is true of Cape Breton.

Pictou has not been the aggressor in this respect so much as Sydney and Inverness.
i	'	.

Will the hon. gentleman allow me to say that so anxious is the Dominion Coal Company at Sydney to obtain this schooner trade that it has standing advertisements in the newspapers calling on schooners to go to Glace Bay, where they have made special arrangements for loading them. They are anxious for this trade, and it is not fair on the part of my hon. friend to say that they are not. The only discrimination of a serious character that has occurred in this connection happened at Inverness last fall, and that is not likely to arise again.

I am not prepared to take the assurances of the hon. member for Pictou nor of the hon. member for Cape Breton ; but I am glad to hear these hon. gentlemen say that some redress has been given to the grievances under which the coasting trade has suffered in the past-However, there is no guarantee that they will be free from such abuses in the future.
What guarantee can you give them ?

You can give them the guarantee that the foreign coasting trade is not to come in to fill their places. The schooners have to lie at Sydney or Inverness for six or eight weeks, waiting for their load, while the steamers load up and carry their cargo up the St. Lawrence and "come back and load up again.
Would you shut up the coal mine ?

There must be some way out. I believe the State of Massaehu-

setts had a law some years ago compelling the vessels to load in rotation, the only exception being that of a steamer which come In for bunker coal. I cannot pick up a paper from the maritime provinces without seeing that the agitation of this question is going on from day to day. Some stringent regulation should be put upon the management of the coal shipping piers, and one of the best ways of rehabilitating our shipping interest is to have a bonus on ship-building so that we may rebuild our shipping and maintain our ships as we did some twenty or twenty-five years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has discussed two questions which are important, but which have no relation to the Bill. The first is with regard to a shipping bounty, a very important question, but it is not involved in this measure at all. If we give a bounty of $50 a ton, we could not get vessels built fast enough to meet the requirements of the coal companies. The second is the difficulty between sailing vessels and steamers at the piers. I believe that difficulty occurred only at one pier at Cape Breton, and I am assured that a remedy has been supplied. But even if there were no remedy, that does not touch the object of this Bill at all. Then my hon. friend says if we only stop these Norwegian steamers, we will have the business for our own vessels. That was his argument.
No, it was not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He wants to shut out these Norwegian steamers altogether. We want to shut them out in a general way, but the coal companies say that if we do not give them reasonable time, they will have no vessels to carry their trade. I represent a constituency which has a good deal of shipping, but if we only carried our coal in the wooden vesesls which we build there, the coal companies could not do a profitable business at all. If they could not use large steamers in carrying their coal, we could not have any coal trade up the St. Lawrence. It is only by building special steamers adapted to the trade, that we can make anything out of it.
Let us build Messager-ies inaritimes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And in the meantime shut up the collieries.
You have not begun any.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, we have launched this day in the town of New Glasgow, a magnificent steel ship and without giving any bonus. It was built by enterprising people and I wish them every success.
But you have not aided them in any way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not going to discuss that question. It may or may not be good policy to aid ship-building. There are certain privileges which have been granted for many years, and whatever advantages there may be in these will go to the splendid steel ship launched by the firm of Carmichael & Co.
Only one steel ship.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, there has to be a beginning to everything.
Since the Minister of Finance is going into a discussion entirely away from the Bill, I rise to a point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is right.
Might I inquire what is the tonnage of this vessel ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: She is quite a good sized vessel.

I do not know that this Bill is much less controversial than the other one we have considered. The subject is a very important one ; but coming back to the immediate purpose of the Bill, perhaps it might be said that its advantages will depend all together on the way it is worked out by orders in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is true.

The Minister of Finance has announced, but only in a very general way, what the policy of the government is likely to be. I would suggest that the Bill might be reported and stand for third reading, on the understanding that if any hon. gentleman who is not present desires further discussion, we can refer it back to the committee.

Might I point out a fact which would perhaps avoid any discussion on the third reading, and that is that in the original Shipping- Act passed in 1870 the power to alter, amend and repeal any order in council that might be passed under the terms of this section were contained in the original Shipping Act. But when they came to revise the statutes in 2 Edward VII., the words giving to the Governor in Council the pow-er to alter, amend and repeal were struck out. The proposition now is only to revive the powers which had previously existed.
Progress reported.
I would like to again bring to the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries the return I mentioned yesterday.

I found out that it had been handed to me some time ago and has been mislaid. I have given instructions to have it recopied and will lay it on the
